Reproducing Figures 1–4 of
Five-dimensional rotating black holes in Einstein–Gauss–Bonnet theory

Y. Brihaye and E. Radu, arXiv:0801.1021, Phys. Lett. B 661 (2008) 167 — report of 2026-09-09. Sources in code/, 31 files.

1. Verdict, and the honest limit of it

The figures were reproduced, in the strict sense. Every curve comes from numerically solving the Einstein–Gauss–Bonnet field equations for the paper's ansatz. Nothing was traced, fitted, or drawn to the published shape. 42 assertions pass, 0 fail.
But "42/42" would be misleading on its own, so: the published figures contain no tabulated numbers and the text quotes none from them. The curves therefore cannot be compared point by point with the originals. What can be compared quantitatively are the exact limits — at $\alpha=0$ the solution must be the Myers–Perry–AdS$_5$ black hole (2.15), at $w_h=0$ the static Gauss–Bonnet black hole (2.14), both closed-form — together with the handful of numbers the paper does print. Those are reproduced to $10^{-8}$. Everything else is agreement of shape, range, monotonicity and endpoints: visual agreement. Two of the four figures (1 and 2) are profile plots, where that is the whole comparison.
And one thing is a real disagreement. Figure 1 is published at $w_h=1.8$. On our branch that value lies past extremality and is not a black hole at all. See §6, which is the most quantitative part of this report.

2. What was actually done

  1. The equations were re-derived. The paper says its reduced equations are “extremely complicated (each of them containing around fifty terms)” and declines to print them, so there was nothing to copy. derive_eqs.py builds the $5\times5$ metric (2.13), the Christoffel symbols, the Riemann tensor, the Gauss–Bonnet tensor $H_{\mu\nu}$ of Eq. (2.4), and six components of Eq. (2.3), with sympy. Runtime ~145 s.
  2. The derivation was verified, not assumed — but it is worth being precise about what each check covers, because they do not cover the same thing:
    • Eq. (2.14), the static Gauss–Bonnet black hole, is a solution for general $\alpha$. Substituting it gives identically zero for all six components, symbolically. This tests the Gauss–Bonnet sector — but only for non-rotating configurations, $w\equiv0$.
    • Eq. (2.15), Myers–Perry–AdS$_5$, is a solution only at $\alpha=0$; it solves Einstein's equations, not the Gauss–Bonnet ones. So it was substituted after setting $\alpha=0$, and gives identically zero there. This tests the rotating sector — but only in the Einstein limit.
    Neither closed form tests the Gauss–Bonnet terms in the presence of rotation — which is precisely the regime the paper is about, and precisely what has no closed form to check against. That gap was left open in the first version of this report. It is now closed empirically, by comparing against the authors' own plotted data: see §5a.
  3. The boundary-value problem was solved by Chebyshev collocation with a Newton/least-squares iteration and an analytic Jacobian, seeded from the closed forms and continued in $\alpha$, $w_h$ and $r_h$ — the strategy described in Section 4 of the paper.
  4. The published quantities were plotted: the same combinations of metric functions in Figures 1 and 2, and the same horizon data, asymptotic coefficients and thermodynamic quantities (Eqs. 3.3, 3.6, 3.7, 3.10) in Figures 3 and 4.

One trick made the symbolic step tractable. Keeping $\theta$ symbolic all the way through a $5\times5$ Riemann tensor does not finish in reasonable time; but the reduced system is $\theta$-independent, so $\theta$ can be fixed to an exact value after the $\theta$-derivatives have been taken. That turns a computation that hangs into one that takes about two and a half minutes.

3. The equations, and what the derivation revealed

With $\Lambda=-6/\ell^2$, Eq. (2.3) reads $R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12 R g_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}+\tfrac{\alpha}{4}H_{\mu\nu}=0$. Three structural facts fell out of the derivation. They were derived, not recalled, and each one is load-bearing for the numerics:

  • No $f''$ occurs anywhere. $f$ is not a dynamical variable.
  • The $(rr)$ component contains no derivative of $f$ at all. It is an algebraic quadratic constraint $a f^2 + c f + d = 0$, and its two roots are the two branches of Gauss–Bonnet gravity (footnote 3 of the paper). The minus branch is the root with a smooth $\alpha\to0$ limit. It satisfies $f(r_h)=0$ whenever $b(r_h)=0$, because once $b$ vanishes every remaining term of the constraint carries a factor of $f$.
  • The rest are linear in $(f',b'',h'',w'')$, as Lovelock's theorem requires.

The $\theta$ check came out more interesting than expected. The $(tt)$, $(rr)$, $(\theta\theta)$, $(t\varphi)$ and $(\varphi\psi)$ components are literally identical at $\theta=\pi/6$ and $\theta=\pi/4$ (the last up to an overall factor of 3). The $(\varphi\varphi)$ component is not, and should not be: $g_{\varphi\varphi}$ itself depends on $\theta$, so that component is a $\theta$-dependent combination of the others. It is still a valid equation at the fixed $\theta$ used, which is how the solver uses it.

Substituting the near-horizon expansion (3.1) shows that the $\varepsilon^0$ and $\varepsilon^1$ coefficients (with $\varepsilon=r-r_h$) vanish identically for the $(tt)$, $(\theta\theta)$ and $(t\varphi)$ components, and that the $(rr)$ component starts at order $\varepsilon$. A non-degenerate horizon with $f=b=0$ is therefore an admissible regular singular point, and the horizon data are constrained only at order $\varepsilon^2$. That degeneracy is the central numerical difficulty of this problem — see §9.

4. The numerical method

Variables. The asymptotics (3.2) are subtracted analytically. With $A=(1-\sqrt{1-2\alpha/\ell^2})/\alpha$,

f = 1 + A r^2 + P(r)/r^2      P -> f2
b = 1 + A r^2 + Q(r)/r^2      Q -> b2
h =     r^2   + Y(r)/r^2      Y -> l^2 (f2-b2)(1+sqrt(1-2a/l^2))/2
w =           Omega(r)/r^4    Omega -> w4

so the asymptotic charges are read off directly instead of being extracted as a cancelling difference of numbers of order $Ar^2\sim10^3$, which at double precision would destroy them.

Grid. Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes in $x\in[0,1]$ with $r=r_h/(1-sx)$, $s=1-r_h/R$; the horizon sits exactly on the first node. The ratio $R/r_h$ sets the dynamic range and it matters: $R=80$, $N=80$ works at $r_h=0.5$ but not at $r_h=0.3$, nor for the fast-rotating solutions. Figures 2 and 3 use $R=80,N=80$; Figures 1 and 4 use $R=30,N=60$.

System. All six derived components are imposed in residual form at every node except the horizon node, where they vanish identically; seven boundary conditions are appended:

f(r_h) = 0     b(r_h) = 0     w(r_h) = w_h
Q'(R) = 0      Omega'(R) = 0   Y'(R) = 0     Y''(R) = 0

$f(r_h)=0$ is what selects the minus branch of the quadratic constraint. Without it the Newton solve converges happily to configurations with $f'(r_h)<0$. The over-determined system is solved in the least-squares sense with an analytic Jacobian (verified against finite differences to $4\times10^{-12}$).

Row scaling. Each equation is a near-perfect cancellation of terms growing like $r^{12}$, so the size of a raw residual says nothing about how strongly that equation constrains the solution. Every row is divided by the norm of its own gradient, frozen during a Newton sweep — and, crucially, each residual is first divided by $(r-r_h)^2$ (by $(r-r_h)$ for the $(rr)$ component) to remove the horizon degeneracy analytically. See §9.

Continuation. From the closed forms — (2.15) when $w_h\neq0$ at $\alpha=0$, (2.14) when $w_h=0$ — then continued in $\alpha$, $w_h$ or $r_h$. For Figure 4, continuation in $r_h$ proved fragile, so each $r_h$ is instead solved independently: seeded from the exact solution at that same $r_h$ and continued in $\alpha$.

5. The figures

5a. Point-by-point against the authors' own data

An earlier version of this report said a point-by-point comparison with the published figures was impossible, because the paper tabulates nothing. That was wrong. The .eps files distributed with the arXiv source are gnuplot 3.7 output: every curve is stored as an absolute x y M followed by relative dx dy V steps, and the axis tick labels are written as text at known device coordinates. The figures therefore contain the numbers, and the axes calibrate from the ticks to a residual of $10^{-16}$. eps_extract.py recovers them; compare_eps.py compares.

Each published curve is matched to one of ours by best agreement, then the RMS difference is taken over the overlapping range and quoted as a fraction of that curve's vertical span:

The overlays are in §5 above: the first shows Figures 3 and 4, the second the profile figures. Figure 2 there is fully like-for-like and the curves lie on top of each other; in Figure 1 only the static curves are at identical parameters, and those coincide as well.

So the reproduction is confirmed quantitatively, not just visually — and this is also the check that closes the gap identified in §2: the Gauss–Bonnet terms with rotation, which no closed form tests, agree with the authors' results to a fraction of a per cent in every asymptotic and thermodynamic quantity.

The exception. $f_1=f'(r_h)$ and $b_1=b'(r_h)$ agree only to 2–3.5%, and $T_H=\sqrt{f_1b_1}/4\pi$ inherits it. Everything else agrees ten to forty times better. A reader noticed the symptom before the cause: in an earlier version those two curves were visibly kinked, i.e. not differentiable in $\alpha$, which the published ones plainly are.

Part of that was ours. Figures 2 and 3 had been computed at $R=80$, and $f_1,b_1$ are by far the quantities most sensitive to how the grid is distributed. Recomputing at $R=30$ removed the kinks and cut the error from ~7% to ~2%, while leaving $f_2$, $b_2$, $w_4$ unchanged in the fifth decimal (third figure in §5). What remained was a smooth, converged 2–3% offset.

5a-i. Is that offset a mistake in our implementation?

Asked directly, and the honest answer is: no test we can construct says so, and two independent tests say the opposite. Neither is conclusive on its own, but together they locate the difficulty in the quantity rather than in either calculation.

Test 1 — the paper's own two figures disagree with each other. Figures 3 and 4 share exactly one solution: $r_h=0.5$, $w_h=0.5$, $\alpha=0.5$, $\ell^2=20$. Figure 3 reaches it at $\alpha=0.5$, Figure 4 at $r_h=0.5$. Reading both off the published .eps files:

$f_1$1.09411.05453.63%1.0643
$b_1$1.35321.31462.85%1.3266
$T_H$0.09690.09363.43%0.0946
$E^{(0)}$0.76070.76810.98%0.7607
$f_2$−0.5202−0.52050.05%−0.5203

The paper disagrees with itself by 3.6% on $f_1$ and 3.4% on $T_H$ at the one point both figures contain — the same size as our disagreement with it — while agreeing with itself to 0.05% on $f_2$, which is also where we agree with it to 0.05%. And our value sits between the paper's own two in every case. The quantities that are hard are hard for both calculations.

Test 2 — the first law. Along Figure 4's family $r_h$ varies at fixed $\alpha$ and fixed $w_h$, so it is a genuine one-parameter family of solutions and must satisfy $dE = T\,dS + 2\Omega\,dJ$ with $\Omega=w_h$; in the paper's plotting units, $dE = 2\pi T\,dS + 2w_h\,dJ$. This is a real test, because $T$ is built from $f_1,b_1$ — the quantities in dispute — while $E$, $S$ and $J$ are built from $f_2$, $b_2$, $w_4$ and $h_h$, on which everyone agrees to better than 1%. Validating the units on the exact $\alpha=0$ family gives a violation of $1.5\times10^{-5}$, which is the floor set by numerical differentiation. Then:

$T$ used, with $E,S,J$ from this workmedian violation of the first law
ours1.2 × 10−5
the published curve4.1 × 10−3

a factor of 340. Inverting the relation, the temperature that $E$, $S$ and $J$ demand agrees with ours to a mean ratio of 1.0000 and with the published curve to 1.0054. Applying the test to the paper's own five curves throughout, with no input from us, the temperature implied by their $E$, $S$, $J$ exceeds their plotted $T$ by 3.7%.

Conclusion. $f_1$ and $b_1$ are simply the hardest quantities in this problem — they are derivatives evaluated at the one point where the field equations degenerate (§3, §9) — and they carry a few per cent of uncertainty in the published calculation as well as in ours. We can find no error in our implementation, our value lies inside the paper's own spread, and the first law independently favours our $T_H$. That is as far as the evidence goes: it is not proof that our number is the right one.

5b. The $f/b$ curve of the published Figure 1 is the reciprocal

A reader noticed that our $f(r)/b(r)$ in Figure 1 rises towards 1 while the published one falls towards 1. It is not a sign error on our side: the published curve behaves like $b/f$.

The argument that relies on nothing but the paper's own figures. When $w_h=0$ the solution is static, $f\equiv b$, and $f/b=1$ — the published Figure 1 shows exactly that for its dashed curve. Switching on rotation, every other panel of the paper puts $f/b$ below 1:

published figureparameters$f/b$ at the horizon
Figure 2$\alpha=1$, $w_h=0.5$0.6707
Figure 2$\alpha=0.1$, $w_h=0.5$0.9638
Figure 3a$\alpha=0.5$, $w_h=0.5$$f_1/b_1=0.8086$
Figure 1$\alpha=0.5$, $w_h=1.8$1.6904

Our own solutions decrease monotonically in $w_h$ — $f_1/b_1 = 1$ at $w_h=0$, 0.66 at $w_h=0.9$, 0.58 at $w_h=1.25$ — so at $w_h=1.8$ one expects a number well below 1, not 1.69. Figure 1 is the only panel that goes the other way.

A second, corroborating handle, with a caveat. Eq. (2.15) has $b=r^2f/h$, so at a horizon where $f$ and $b$ vanish linearly, $f/b|_{r_h} = h_h/r_h^2$. Figure 1's own $h/r^2+1$ curve reads 1.5913 at the horizon, i.e. $h_h/r_h^2 = 0.5913$, and $1/0.5913 = 1.6911$ — the plotted curve (1.6904) to 0.04%. The caveat: that relation is exact only at $\alpha=0$. We never impose it (see §5c), and at $\alpha=0.5$ our solutions violate it by about 4%. So a 0.04% match to its reciprocal is in fact too good, which suggests the curve may have been generated as $r^2/h$ rather than as an independently computed $b/f$. Either way it is not $f/b$.

We read this as a plotting or labelling slip confined to that one panel: Figures 2 and 3a of the same paper use the convention we do, and the field equations fix which way up it goes. It is the authors' figure, so we set out the evidence and leave the conclusion to the reader. Inverting our curve would reproduce the published shape.

5c. Is $b=r^2f/h$ assumed for $\alpha\neq0$?

No — it is never used anywhere in the solver. $b$ is an independent unknown function, discretised on the same grid as $f$, $h$ and $w$ and determined by its own field equation. The relation is a property of the exact Myers–Perry–AdS$_5$ solution (2.15), which solves the equations only at $\alpha=0$.

What happens once $\alpha\neq0$ is therefore a result, and it is worth recording, because it measures how far the Gauss–Bonnet solutions move away from the Einstein ones:

$\alpha$$f_1/b_1$$h_h/r_h^2$violation
01.065791.06579$1\times10^{-8}$ (exact)
0.20.908170.938373.2%
0.50.802230.837964.3%
1.00.649150.713289.0%

Through the bulk rather than at the horizon, $|b-r^2f/h|/|b|$ reaches 5.9% at $\alpha=1$ and 2.0% at $\alpha=0.1$. That the violation vanishes to $10^{-8}$ at $\alpha=0$, where it must, is one more check that the solver is doing what it claims.

6. Why $w_h=1.8$ could not be reached

The short version, without any numerics. Spin a black hole faster while holding its horizon radius fixed and you drain its surface gravity. In Kerr this is the familiar bound $a\le M$: past it there is no horizon left, only a naked singularity. The same thing happens here. The horizon velocity $w_h$ cannot be raised indefinitely at fixed $r_h$ — at some $w_h^{\rm ext}$ the temperature $T_H\propto\sqrt{f'(r_h)b'(r_h)}$ reaches zero, the horizon becomes degenerate, and beyond that no black hole with that $r_h$ exists for the solver to find. So the failure to reach $w_h=1.8$ is not a case of the solver giving up on a hard problem; on our branch there is nothing there to converge to.
Two things then blur together near the wall, and they are worth separating. Physically, the family ends. Numerically, our accuracy dies just before it ends, because $f_1,b_1\to0$ makes the near-horizon rows — already the delicate part of this discretisation (§9) — degenerate further. So our practical limit sits a little inside the true one: at $\alpha=0$ the true bound is 1.4318 and we stop trusting ourselves around 1.40–1.43.

At fixed $r_h$ the family of black holes ends at an extremal horizon velocity, where $f'(r_h),b'(r_h)\to0$ and $T_H\to0$; past it $f'(r_h)<0$ and $r=r_h$ is no longer an outer horizon.

At $\alpha=0$ this needs no numerics at all, because the family is the exact solution (2.15). For $r_h=0.5$, $\ell^2=20$ it becomes extremal at $\hat a = 0.353526$, that is at

$w_h^{\rm ext} = 1.431782$

so at $\alpha=0$, $w_h=1.8$ is not a black hole. The question is then whether the solver's failure is its own, and whether $\alpha$ moves the bound.

Is the solver at fault? No. Compared against the exact family right up to the bound:

Does $\alpha$ move the bound? Barely. At $\alpha=0.5$, the parameters of Figure 1, $f_1$ and $b_1$ decrease monotonically and both cross zero between $w_h=1.45$ and $1.50$:

Conclusion. On our branch, $w_h=1.8$ at $r_h=0.5$, $\alpha=0.5$, $\ell^2=20$ lies beyond extremality. We cannot tell whether the paper normalises $w$ differently, sits on a different branch, or whether our continuation leaves the physical branch early. The discrepancy is recorded as unresolved; we do not assert the paper is wrong on the strength of our own numerics. Figure 1 is drawn at $w_h=1.25$, the largest value at which every field equation still holds to $10^{-6}$ relative.

A caution about method, from the same investigation: the same polynomial extrapolation that nails the $\alpha=0$ bound to five digits returns nan at $\alpha=0.5$, and $f_1$/$b_1$ estimates differing by 50% at $\alpha=0.25$. Those numbers are not quoted anywhere; the $\alpha=0.5$ statement above rests on direct bracketing, not extrapolation. A method that passes one validation is not thereby validated everywhere.

7. Accuracy, measured not assumed

Solving the same configuration ($r_h=0.5$, $w_h=0.5$, $\alpha=0.5$) at two outer radii:

--- effect of the outer radius, at r_h = 0.5, alpha = 0.5, w_h = 0.5
    R=  30 N= 60  f1=1.064271 b1=1.326642 hh=0.209491 f2=-0.520314 b2=-0.520330 w4=0.062000
    R=  80 N= 80  f1=1.013254 b1=1.393137 hh=0.209394 f2=-0.520259 b2=-0.520274 w4=0.061981
    f1  relative difference 5.03e-02

$f_2$, $b_2$, $h_h$ and $w_4$ agree to a few parts in $10^4$. But $f_1$ and $b_1$ individually differ by about 5% — while their product, which is what $T_H$ depends on, agrees to $2\times10^{-4}$. So the $f_1$ and $b_1$ curves in Figures 3a and 4a carry a few per cent of numerical uncertainty and every other plotted quantity is good to $\sim10^{-4}$. The paper reports $10^{-8}$ relative accuracy for its own collocation solutions; we are not there.

8. What was not reproduced, and not checked

Not reproduced.

  • Figure 1 at $w_h=1.8$ — §6. Drawn at $w_h=1.25$.
  • Figure 4 below $r_h\approx0.3$. The published figure starts near $r_h=0.15$; our solves below 0.30 fail the linearity test at the horizon. The paper itself notes that “for small values of $r_h$ the numerical analysis is quite tedious”.
  • The two-branch structure in $w_h$ described at the end of Section 4.

Not checked.

  • No point-by-point comparison with the published curves is possible: the paper tabulates nothing.
  • Figures 3 and 4 are drawn with the published axis limits, so a curve that leaves the frame does so here and not necessarily in the original.
  • The counterterm coefficients $c_1,c_2$ of Eq. (2.9) and the boundary stress tensor (2.10)–(2.11) were not re-derived; deriving them needs the boundary variational calculus, not the bulk equations. The charge formulas (3.6)–(3.7) are used as the paper gives them. What is checked is that they return the exact Casimir energy $3\ell^2/8$ at $\alpha=0$ and the closed-form static entropy $S=r_h^3+3\alpha r_h$.

9. Five bugs, and the one that bit three times

Recorded because each one produced plausible-looking output, and because the last is a trap anyone solving this system will fall into.

  1. Wrong index placement in $H_{\mu\nu}$ — a bug in our sympy code. To be explicit, since this is about our program and not about the paper: Eq. (2.4) contains the term $R_{\mu\sigma\kappa\tau}R_\nu{}^{\sigma\kappa\tau}$, in which the second factor has its first index down and the last three up. In derive_eqs.py we first built that factor from an array holding $R^{\nu p}{}_{qu}$ — i.e. with the first two indices raised — instead of taking $R_{\nu p q u}$ and raising only the last three. The correction is the single line now reading B = sum(Ginv[s_,p]*Rdn[nu,p,q,u]*Ginv[k,q]*Ginv[tt,u] ...), where Rdn is the fully lowered Riemann tensor.
    Symptom: the derived equations came out quadratic in the second derivatives, which violates the quasi-linearity Lovelock's theorem guarantees. Caught by a numerical linearity test (second differences in $b''$, $h''$, $w''$ should vanish), not by reading the code. After the fix the equations shrank from ~2800 to ~170 operations for the $(rr)$ component, and the closed-form solutions satisfied them identically.
  2. Wrong horizon mass for the static solution — again our code, since corrected. This entry describes a bug we made and then fixed; the wrong expression below is not what the code does now, which has caused confusion, so both are spelled out.

    Eq. (2.14) is $f = 1 + \frac{r^2}{\alpha}\left(1-\sqrt{1+2\alpha\left(\frac{m}{r^4}-\frac{1}{\ell^2}\right)}\right)$, and to build the static starting configuration we need the $m$ that puts the horizon at $r_h$, i.e. that solves $f(r_h)=0$. Rearranging, $\frac{r_h^2}{\alpha}\left(\sqrt{\cdot}-1\right)=1$, so
    what we first coded (wrong):   $\sqrt{\;\cdot\;} = 1 + \dfrac{r_h^{2}}{\alpha}$
    what it should be, and what the code does now:   $\sqrt{\;\cdot\;} = 1 + \dfrac{\alpha}{r_h^{2}}$
    The corrected version is the one obtained by hand by a reader of this report, and sympy confirms it: solving $f(r_h)=0$ symbolically gives the closed form
    $m = \dfrac{\alpha}{2} + r_h^{2} + \dfrac{r_h^{4}}{\ell^{2}}$
    which is exactly what egb_exact.static_gb_horizon_mass computes, and $f(r_h)$ evaluates to $0$ to $10^{-16}$ at every parameter set tested (scratch/audit_inversions.py). The analogous inversion for MPAdS$_5$ was audited the same way and is correct.
    Symptom of the original bug: the static seed was not a solution at all, so every $w_h$ continuation started from the wrong configuration. It was caught by comparing the "static" solve against the closed form.
  3. The branch condition was missing. $b(r_h)=0$ alone leaves both roots of the quadratic constraint available; the solver returned $f'(r_h)<0$ with a tiny residual. Fixed by imposing $f(r_h)=0$ explicitly — in the $(rr)$ row at the horizon node, which is vacuous there anyway.
  4. Grid transfer during $r_h$ continuation. Interpolating the previous solution in $r$ smears the horizon region and throws Newton onto an unphysical branch. Since consecutive grids share the same computational nodes $x$, the correct transfer is the identity in $x$.
  5. The outer radius. $R/r_h$ is the grid's dynamic range; $R=80$ silently degrades at $r_h=0.3$.
The one that bit three times. Three separate times the solver reported residuals of $10^{-20}$ – $10^{-25}$ together with horizon data that were pure noise ($f_1=-16$, $b_1=47$, $h_h<0$), or with $f$ and $b$ sitting at $10^{-12}$ over the first several nodes instead of vanishing linearly.

Every time the cause was the same shape of error: the rows near the horizon carry no weight, because every field equation vanishes like $(r-r_h)^2$ there. Normalising residuals by their own magnitude, or putting a floor under that scale, silently deletes exactly the equations that pin the horizon. Remove the floor and the solver instead fits amplified round-off.

The cure is to divide the zero out analytically — each residual by $(r-r_h)^2$, the $(rr)$ one by $(r-r_h)$ — and only then equilibrate rows by the norm of their own gradient.

The lesson worth keeping: a tiny residual is not evidence of a solution when the residual has been normalised by something that itself vanishes. The diagnostic that actually caught it was not the residual at all, but checking that $f(r)/(r-r_h) \to f'(r_h)$ near the horizon.

A related trap, found later: that same linearity diagnostic fails legitimately near extremality, because $f_1\to0$ makes higher-order terms dominate at any fixed node. Used as a rejection test it was over-conservative and threw away good solutions. Tests have domains of validity too.

PASS F3  the published T_H fits that same first law far less well median violation: ours 1.2e-05, theirs 4.1e-03
PASS F4  the paper's Fig 3a and Fig 4a disagree on f1 at their shared solution Fig3a 1.0941 vs Fig4a 1.0545  (3.63%)
PASS F5  our f1 lies between the paper's own two values         ours 1.0643, theirs 1.0545 and 1.0941

--- G. the relation b = r^2 f / h ---

Appendix. The numerical method, in plain terms

A.1 What has to be solved

After the reduction, the unknowns are four functions of one variable, $f,b,h,w$ on $r\in[r_h,\infty)$. Three of the equations are second order in $b,h,w$; $f$ is fixed pointwise by the algebraic $(rr)$ constraint. This is a boundary-value problem, not an initial-value one: conditions are imposed at both ends (regularity and $w=w_h$ at the horizon, prescribed asymptotics at infinity), so one cannot simply integrate outward from $r_h$.

A.2 Why not just shoot?

The obvious method is shooting: guess the missing horizon data, integrate outward with a Runge–Kutta solver, see how badly you miss the conditions at infinity, adjust, repeat. Two things spoil it here. First, $r=r_h$ is a singular point of the system: $f$ and $b$ both vanish there, and writing the equations in the explicit form $y'=g(y)$ requires inverting a matrix that becomes singular exactly at the horizon (we measured its condition number blowing up like $1/\varepsilon^2$). Second, the unwanted asymptotic modes grow with $r$, so small errors at the horizon are amplified on the way out.

A.3 Collocation: turn the ODEs into algebra

Collocation avoids both. Instead of marching, you represent each unknown function by its values at a fixed set of points — here $N+1$ Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes, which cluster towards the ends of the interval. Derivatives at those nodes are then linear combinations of the values: a single dense matrix $D$ with $u'\approx Du$, exact for polynomials up to degree $N$ and spectrally accurate for smooth functions. Substituting into the field equations turns each differential equation, at each node, into one algebraic equation. The whole boundary-value problem becomes one large system of nonlinear algebraic equations in the $4(N+1)$ unknown nodal values — and because the horizon is just another node where the (polynomial) equations are perfectly finite, the singularity is no longer an obstacle.

A.3a What exactly are $P$, $Q$, $Y$, $\Omega$? (they are not constants)

A natural misreading, worth heading off. Eq. (3.2) says $f = 1 + Ar^2 + f_2/r^2 + O(1/r^4)$, and we define $P$ by $f = 1 + Ar^2 + P(r)/r^2$. It can look as though $P$ has been defined to be the constant $f_2$. It has not.

$P$, $Q$, $Y$ and $\Omega$ are unknown functions of $r$, carried as $N+1$ nodal values each, exactly like $f,b,h,w$ themselves. Eq. (3.2) is only the leading asymptotic behaviour, so what is true is $$P(r) = f_2 + \frac{f_4}{r^2} + \dots \xrightarrow[r\to\infty]{} f_2 ,$$ a limit, not an identity. At finite $r$, and especially near the horizon, $P$ varies a great deal: $f(r_h)=0$ forces $P(r_h) = -r_h^2(1+Ar_h^2)$, which is a definite non-zero number fixed by the horizon condition. For the $\alpha=1$ solution of Figure 2, for instance,

$r$0.5000.5350.6630.9841.90530.0
$P(r)$−0.2532−0.2846−0.3941 −0.5997−0.7674−0.7900

— a factor of three between the horizon and the outer boundary, flattening onto $f_2=-0.7897$ only at the far end. The substitution is a change of variables, not an ansatz: it buys two things and assumes nothing. It makes the unknowns $O(1)$ instead of $O(r^2)$, and it puts the quantity we actually want, $f_2$, at a single node ($P$ at $r=R$) instead of requiring us to extract it from the difference of two large nearly-cancelling numbers. The boundary conditions $Q'(R)=\Omega'(R)=Y'(R)=0$ are precisely the statement "these functions have gone flat by the outer boundary", i.e. that the asymptotic regime has been reached — and they would be vacuous if the functions were constants by construction.

A.4 Newton, and what a "Newton sweep" means here

First, what a "row" is. After collocation the whole problem is one vector equation $F(u)=0$. The unknown vector is $$u = \big(P_0,\dots,P_N,\;Q_0,\dots,Q_N,\;Y_0,\dots,Y_N,\;\Omega_0,\dots,\Omega_N\big) \in\mathbb{R}^{4(N+1)},$$ the nodal values. The residual $F(u)$ is built like this: from $u$ we reconstruct $f,b,h,w$ and their derivatives at every node, using the definitions (S) for the values and the differentiation matrix $D$ for the derivatives; we substitute those into the left-hand side of each of the six derived field equations; and we collect the results. So

$F_i(u) \;=\;$ (equation $k$, evaluated at node $j$),   divided by $(r_j-r_h)^2$ and by its row weight,

with one such entry for every pair $(k,j)$, plus seven further entries holding the boundary conditions (BC). A row is one of these scalar entries — one equation at one point — and correspondingly one row of the Jacobian $J_{i m}=\partial F_i/\partial u_m$. Solving the discretised problem means finding $u$ with $F(u)=0$, and since there are more rows than unknowns (six equations per node, four unknowns per node) we minimise $\|F(u)\|^2$ instead.

Why "the rows near the horizon carry no weight". Least squares minimises $\sum_i \big(F_i/w_i\big)^2$, so a row divided by a large weight $w_i$ contributes almost nothing to the sum: the solver is then free to violate that equation at no cost. Now, every field equation vanishes like $(r-r_h)^2$ at the horizon, so at the nodes nearest $r_h$ the raw residuals are tiny whatever the solution looks like there. Scale each row by its own magnitude and put a floor under the scale — which is what we did, twice — and those rows get divided by something far larger than themselves; they drop out of the sum, and the near-horizon part of the solution becomes unconstrained. That is exactly the failure in §9: residuals of $10^{-25}$ next to horizon data that were noise. Remove the floor instead and the same rows are divided by something vanishing, which amplifies round-off to $O(1)$ and the solver fits the noise. Neither extreme works; the cure is to cancel the $(r-r_h)^2$ analytically first, and only then scale each row by the norm of its own gradient, which measures how strongly that equation constrains $u$ rather than how big it happens to be.

Newton. With $F$ defined, Newton's method linearises about the current guess, $F(u+\delta)\approx F(u)+J\delta$, solves $J\delta=-F(u)$ in the least-squares sense, steps to $u+\delta$, and repeats until $F$ is at round-off. We supply $J$ analytically — the chain rule through (S) and through $D$ — which is both faster and more accurate than finite-differencing some 250 columns; it agrees with a central-difference Jacobian to $4\times10^{-12}$.

Now the phrase itself. The row scaling just described depends on the solution, and letting it change during the iteration would destroy Newton's quadratic convergence — the residual would no longer be a fixed function being driven to zero. So the weights are computed once, held frozen while Newton iterates to convergence, then recomputed from the new solution, and Newton run again. One such cycle — freeze the weights, iterate Newton to convergence, recompute the weights — is what is meant here by a "Newton sweep". Three sweeps are used; in practice the solution stops moving after the second.

A.5 Continuation

Newton only converges from a good enough starting guess, and for these equations there is no good guess at, say, $\alpha=1$. So we start where an exact solution is known — Eq. (2.15) at $\alpha=0$, or Eq. (2.14) at $w_h=0$ — and walk the parameter in small steps, each solve seeded with the previous answer. This is the standard trick, and it is what the paper describes doing in its Section 4. It also explains a failure mode we hit: if a step is too large, or if the transfer between grids is sloppy, Newton converges to a different solution of the same equations — one that is mathematically valid but not a black hole (see the $f'(r_h)<0$ branch in §9).

A.6 What this method does not give you

It gives no error estimate. A converged Newton solve says the residual is at round-off for the discretisation you chose; it says nothing about whether that discretisation resolves the problem. All the accuracy statements in this report therefore come from outside the solver: comparison with closed-form solutions, variation of $N$ and $R$, and comparison with the authors' published data.

11. The source files
