      margin:2rem auto;padding:0 1rem;color:#1a1a1a}}
 h1{{font-size:1.6rem;line-height:1.3}} h2{{margin-top:2.2rem;border-bottom:1px solid #ddd;
    padding-bottom:.2rem}} h3{{margin:.3rem 0}}
 pre{{background:#f6f6f6;padding:.8rem;overflow-x:auto;font-size:12px;border-radius:4px}}
 table{{border-collapse:collapse;margin:1rem 0;width:100%}}
 td,th{{border:1px solid #ddd;padding:.35rem .6rem;text-align:left;font-size:14px}}
 th{{background:#f0f0f0}}
 img{{max-width:100%;border:1px solid #eee}}
 figure{{margin:1.5rem 0}} figcaption{{font-size:13px;color:#555;margin-top:.3rem}}
 .verdict{{background:#eef7ee;border-left:4px solid #4a4;padding:.8rem 1rem;margin:1rem 0}}
 .caveat{{background:#fff8e6;border-left:4px solid #e9a;padding:.8rem 1rem;margin:1rem 0}}
 code{{background:#f0f0f0;padding:1px 4px;border-radius:3px}}
</style>

<h1>Reproducing Figures 1&ndash;4 of<br>
<em>Five-dimensional rotating black holes in Einstein&ndash;Gauss&ndash;Bonnet theory</em></h1>
<p>Y. Brihaye and E. Radu, <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/0801.1021">arXiv:0801.1021</a>,
Phys. Lett. B <b>661</b> (2008) 167. &mdash; run of {date}.</p>

<div class="verdict">
<b>Verdict: the figures were {verdict}.</b>
The curves come from numerically solving the Einstein&ndash;Gauss&ndash;Bonnet field
equations for the paper's ansatz. They were not traced, fitted, or drawn to
match the published shapes. {npass} assertions pass and {nfail} fail.
</div>

<div class="box good" style="background:#eef7ee;border-left:4px solid #4a4;padding:.8rem 1rem;margin:1rem 0">
<b>Compared point by point with the authors' own data.</b> The .eps files in the
arXiv source are gnuplot output and contain the plotted coordinates, so the
published curves can be recovered as numbers (<code>eps_extract.py</code>). Every
curve of Figures 3 and 4 agrees: $f_2$, $b_2$, $w_4$ to 0.05&ndash;0.2% of span,
$E^{{(0)}}$, $J$, $S_0$, $S_{{GB}}$, $E^{{(c)}}$ to below 0.8%, $h_h$ to 0.85%. The
exception is $f_1$ and $b_1$ (and $T_H$, built from them) at 2&ndash;3.5%.
</div>

<div class="caveat">
<b>The remaining limit of that claim.</b> Figures 1 and 2 are profile plots whose
published versions are partly clipped by their own axes, so those are compared
only in range and shape. What <em>can</em> be, and is, checked
quantitatively are the exact limits: at $\alpha=0$ the solution must be the
Myers&ndash;Perry&ndash;AdS$_5$ black hole (2.15) and at $w_h=0$ the static
Gauss&ndash;Bonnet black hole (2.14), both known in closed form, and the paper
prints $\hat M$, $\hat a$ (footnote 10) and the coefficients $f_2,b_2,w_4$
(footnote 4) for exactly the parameters used in Figures 3 and 4. Those are
reproduced to $10^{{-8}}$. Note also what the closed forms do <em>not</em> cover:
(2.14) tests the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet sector without rotation, (2.15) tests rotation
only at $\alpha=0$, so neither tests the two together &mdash; the regime the paper
is about. That gap is closed by the comparison with the published data above.
</div>

<h2>What was actually done</h2>
<ol>
<li><b>The equations were re-derived.</b> The paper says the reduced equations are
&ldquo;extremely complicated (each of them containing around fifty terms)&rdquo;
and does not print them. <code>derive_eqs.py</code> therefore builds the metric
(2.13), its Christoffel symbols, Riemann tensor, the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet tensor
$H_{{\mu\nu}}$ of Eq. (2.4), and six components of Eq. (2.3), with computer
algebra. Nothing about the equations was taken from the paper or recalled.</li>
<li><b>The derivation was verified</b> by substituting the paper's two closed-form
solutions, Eqs. (2.14) and (2.15), into the derived equations: both give
identically zero, symbolically.</li>
<li><b>Structure found by the derivation</b> (not stated in the paper): no $f''$
occurs; the $(rr)$ component is an algebraic quadratic constraint on $f$, whose
two roots are the two Gauss&ndash;Bonnet branches; the other components are
linear in $(f',b'',h'',w'')$; and near the horizon all components vanish to
order $\varepsilon^2$, so the horizon is a regular singular point.</li>
<li><b>The boundary-value problem was solved</b> by Chebyshev collocation with a
Newton/least-squares iteration and an analytic Jacobian, with the asymptotics of
Eq. (3.2) subtracted analytically so that $f_2$, $b_2$ and $w_4$ are read off
directly rather than extracted from a cancelling difference. Solutions are
started from the closed forms and continued in $\alpha$, $w_h$ and $r_h$ &mdash;
the strategy of Section 4 of the paper.</li>
<li><b>The published quantities were plotted</b>: the same combinations of metric
functions in Figures 1 and 2, and the same horizon data, asymptotic coefficients
and thermodynamic quantities (Eqs. 3.3, 3.6, 3.7, 3.10) in Figures 3 and 4.</li>
</ol>

<h2>Quantitative comparison with the numbers the paper prints</h2>
{table}

<h2>The figures</h2>
{figs}

<h2>What was <em>not</em> reproduced</h2>
<ul>
<li><b>Figure 1 at $w_h=1.8$ &mdash; and this one appears to be a real
discrepancy, not just a numerical shortfall.</b> At fixed $r_h$ the family of
black holes ends at an <em>extremal</em> horizon velocity, where
$f'(r_h),b'(r_h)\to0$ and $T_H\to0$. At $\alpha=0$ that bound is known in
closed form: for $r_h=0.5$, $\ell^2=20$ the Myers&ndash;Perry&ndash;AdS$_5$
family becomes extremal at $\hat a=0.3535$, i.e. at
<b>$w_h=1.431782$</b>. Our numerics reproduce the exact family to $10^{{-8}}$ up
to $w_h=1.2$ and to $1.4\times10^{{-4}}$ at $w_h=1.40$, so this bound is not an
artefact. Switching on $\alpha=0.5$ moves it only a little: $f_1$ and $b_1$ both
cross zero between $w_h=1.45$ and $1.50$. On our branch, then, $w_h=1.8$ is past
the extremal limit and is not a black hole at all. We cannot say whether the
paper uses a different normalisation of $w$, a different branch, or whether our
continuation leaves the physical branch early; the discrepancy is unresolved.
Figure 1 is therefore drawn at $w_h=1.25$, the largest value at which every
field equation still holds to $10^{{-6}}$ relative.</li>
<li><b>Figure 4 below $r_h\approx0.3$.</b> The published figure starts near
$r_h=0.15$; our solves below 0.30 fail the same linearity test. The paper itself
notes that &ldquo;for small values of $r_h$ the numerical analysis is quite
tedious&rdquo;.</li>
<li>The two-branch structure in $w_h$ described at the end of Section 4.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Accuracy &mdash; measured, not assumed</h2>
<p>Solving the same configuration ($r_h=0.5$, $w_h=0.5$, $\alpha=0.5$) at outer
radius $R=30$ and at $R=80$ changes $f_2$ and $b_2$ by $1\times10^{{-4}}$ relative,
$h_h$ by $5\times10^{{-4}}$, $w_4$ by $3\times10^{{-4}}$ &mdash; but changes $f_1$ and
$b_1$ individually by about <b>5%</b>, while their <em>product</em>, which is what
$T_H$ depends on, agrees to $2\times10^{{-4}}$. So the $f_1$ and $b_1$ curves in
Figures 3a and 4a carry a few per cent of numerical uncertainty; every other
plotted quantity is good to a few parts in $10^4$. That is short of the
$10^{{-8}}$ the paper reports for its own solutions.</p>

<h2>What was not checked</h2>
<ul>
<li>No point-by-point comparison with the published curves is possible: the paper
tabulates nothing.</li>
<li>Figures 1 and 2 are profile plots; away from the $\alpha\to0$ and $w_h\to0$
limits their agreement with the originals is visual only.</li>
<li>Figures 3 and 4 are drawn with the published axis limits, so a curve that
leaves the frame does so here and not necessarily in the original.</li>
<li>The counterterm coefficients $c_1,c_2$ of Eq. (2.9) and the boundary stress
tensor (2.10) were not re-derived here; the charge formulas (3.6)&ndash;(3.7) are
used as the paper gives them. What is checked is that they return the exact
Casimir energy $3\ell^2/8$ at $\alpha=0$ and the closed-form static entropy
$S=r_h^3+3\alpha r_h$.</li>
</ul>

<h2>Assertion output</h2>
<pre>{assertions}</pre>

<h2>Run log &mdash; figures</h2>
<pre>{runlog}</pre>

<h2>Run log &mdash; symbolic derivation</h2>
<pre>{derivelog}</pre>
"""

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

"""Build a standalone bundle in ../egb0801-report/ :

    index.html   the full commentary on this reproduction -- what was done, what
                 was checked, what was not, the bugs, and the w_h = 1.8
                 investigation -- with the figures embedded and every source
                 file included inline
    code/*.py    the actual Python files, copied

The HTML embeds the figures as data URIs and the sources as text, so the page
works on its own; only the MathJax formula rendering needs the network.
"""
import base64
import datetime
import html
import os
import shutil

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
OUT = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(HERE), 'egb0801-report')

SOURCES = [

     'The paper does not print them.'),

     'the derived equations; both must vanish identically.'),

     'gradients and row scalings.'),

    ('make_figures.py', 'Figures 1-3 (and a fragile r_h continuation for '
     'Figure 4, superseded by refine.py).'),

     'r_h, plus the R = 30 vs R = 80 accuracy cross-check.'),

    ('emit_tables.py', 'Writes numbers.tex so the write-up cannot drift from '
     'the run.'),
    ('make_report.py', 'Builds report.html.'),

FIGS = [('fig_overlay.png', 'Overlay: this work vs the published curves '
         '(Figures 3 and 4)',

        ('fig_overlay_profiles.png', 'Overlay: the profile figures (1 and 2)',

         '$R=80$ computation, blue the corrected $R=30$ one, grey the authors\' '

         'not move in the fifth decimal between the two.'),

         '$0.30\\le r_h\\le1.00$; the paper starts near 0.15.')]


def read(path, limit=None):
    p = os.path.join(HERE, path)
    if not os.path.exists(p):
        return '(missing: %s)' % path
    with open(p, 'rb') as fh:
        t = fh.read().decode('utf8', 'replace')
    return t if limit is None else t[:limit]


def b64(path):
    with open(os.path.join(HERE, path), 'rb') as fh:
        return base64.b64encode(fh.read()).decode()


def main():
    os.makedirs(os.path.join(OUT, 'code'), exist_ok=True)
    copied = []
    for rel, _ in SOURCES:
        src = os.path.join(HERE, rel)
        if not os.path.exists(src):
            continue
        dst = os.path.join(OUT, 'code', os.path.basename(rel))
        shutil.copy2(src, dst)
        copied.append(rel)
    for extra in ('README.md', 'run_log.txt', 'assert.log', 'writeup.tex',
                  'writeup.pdf', 'figdata.npz', 'egb_notebook.html'):
        p = os.path.join(HERE, extra)
        if os.path.exists(p):
            shutil.copy2(p, os.path.join(OUT, extra))

    figs = ''
    for fn, title, cap in FIGS:
        if not os.path.exists(os.path.join(HERE, fn)):
            continue
        figs += ('<figure><h3>%s</h3><img src="data:image/png;base64,%s" alt="%s">'
                 '<figcaption>%s</figcaption></figure>' % (title, b64(fn), title, cap))

    code = ''
    for rel in copied:
        desc = dict(SOURCES)[rel]
        body = html.escape(read(rel))
        n = body.count('\n') + 1
        code += ('<details><summary><code>%s</code> &mdash; %s '
                 '<span class="n">(%d lines)</span></summary>'
                 '<pre class="src">%s</pre></details>'
                 % (html.escape(rel), html.escape(desc), n, body))

    subs = {
        'date': datetime.date.today().isoformat(),
        'figs': figs, 'code': code, 'nfiles': str(len(copied)),
        'assertions': html.escape(read('assert.log')),
        'runlog': html.escape(read('run_log.txt')),
        'whacc': html.escape(read('scratch/whacc.log')),
        'fig1wh': html.escape(read('scratch/fig1_wh.log')),
        'crosscheck': html.escape('\n'.join(read('refine.log').splitlines()[:9])),
    }
    page = TEMPLATE
    for k, v in subs.items():
        page = page.replace('@@%s@@' % k, v)
    with open(os.path.join(OUT, 'index.html'), 'w') as fh:
        fh.write(page)
    print('wrote %s/index.html  (%d source files in code/)' % (OUT, len(copied)))

<h2 id="verdict">1. Verdict, and the honest limit of it</h2>

<div class="box good">
<b>The figures were reproduced, in the strict sense.</b> Every curve comes from
numerically solving the Einstein&ndash;Gauss&ndash;Bonnet field equations for the
paper's ansatz. Nothing was traced, fitted, or drawn to the published shape.
<b>42 assertions pass, 0 fail.</b>
</div>

<div class="box warn">
<b>But "42/42" would be misleading on its own, so:</b> the published figures
contain no tabulated numbers and the text quotes none from them. The curves
therefore <em>cannot</em> be compared point by point with the originals. What can
be compared quantitatively are the exact limits &mdash; at $\alpha=0$ the solution
must be the Myers&ndash;Perry&ndash;AdS$_5$ black hole (2.15), at $w_h=0$ the
static Gauss&ndash;Bonnet black hole (2.14), both closed-form &mdash; together with
the handful of numbers the paper does print. Those are reproduced to
$10^{-8}$. Everything else is agreement of shape, range, monotonicity and
endpoints: visual agreement. Two of the four figures (1 and 2) are profile plots,
where that is the whole comparison.
</div>

<div class="box bad">
<b>And one thing is a real disagreement.</b> Figure 1 is published at $w_h=1.8$.
On our branch that value lies <em>past extremality</em> and is not a black hole at
all. See &sect;6, which is the most quantitative part of this report.
</div>

<h2 id="did">2. What was actually done</h2>
<ol>
<li><b>The equations were re-derived.</b> The paper says its reduced equations are
&ldquo;extremely complicated (each of them containing around fifty terms)&rdquo;
and declines to print them, so there was nothing to copy.
<code>derive_eqs.py</code> builds the $5\times5$ metric (2.13), the Christoffel
symbols, the Riemann tensor, the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet tensor $H_{\mu\nu}$ of
Eq. (2.4), and six components of Eq. (2.3), with sympy. Runtime ~145 s.</li>
<li><b>The derivation was verified, not assumed</b> &mdash; but it is worth being
precise about <em>what</em> each check covers, because they do not cover the same
thing:
<ul>
<li>Eq. <b>(2.14)</b>, the static Gauss&ndash;Bonnet black hole, is a solution for
<em>general</em> $\alpha$. Substituting it gives identically zero for all six
components, symbolically. This tests the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet sector &mdash; but only
for non-rotating configurations, $w\equiv0$.</li>
<li>Eq. <b>(2.15)</b>, Myers&ndash;Perry&ndash;AdS$_5$, is a solution <em>only at
$\alpha=0$</em>; it solves Einstein's equations, not the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet ones.
So it was substituted after setting $\alpha=0$, and gives identically zero there.
This tests the rotating sector &mdash; but only in the Einstein limit.</li>
</ul>
<b>Neither closed form tests the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet terms in the presence of
rotation</b> &mdash; which is precisely the regime the paper is about, and precisely
what has no closed form to check against. That gap was left open in the first
version of this report. It is now closed empirically, by comparing against the
authors' own plotted data: see &sect;5a.</li>
<li><b>The boundary-value problem was solved</b> by Chebyshev collocation with a
Newton/least-squares iteration and an analytic Jacobian, seeded from the closed
forms and continued in $\alpha$, $w_h$ and $r_h$ &mdash; the strategy described in
Section 4 of the paper.</li>
<li><b>The published quantities were plotted</b>: the same combinations of metric
functions in Figures 1 and 2, and the same horizon data, asymptotic coefficients
and thermodynamic quantities (Eqs. 3.3, 3.6, 3.7, 3.10) in Figures 3 and 4.</li>
</ol>

<p>One trick made the symbolic step tractable. Keeping $\theta$ symbolic all the
way through a $5\times5$ Riemann tensor does not finish in reasonable time; but
the reduced system is $\theta$-independent, so $\theta$ can be fixed to an exact
value <em>after</em> the $\theta$-derivatives have been taken. That turns a
computation that hangs into one that takes about two and a half minutes.</p>

<h2 id="eqs">3. The equations, and what the derivation revealed</h2>

<p>With $\Lambda=-6/\ell^2$, Eq. (2.3) reads
$R_{\mu\nu}-\tfrac12 R g_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}+\tfrac{\alpha}{4}H_{\mu\nu}=0$.
Three structural facts fell out of the derivation. They were <em>derived</em>, not
recalled, and each one is load-bearing for the numerics:</p>

<ul>
<li><b>No $f''$ occurs anywhere.</b> $f$ is not a dynamical variable.</li>
<li><b>The $(rr)$ component contains no derivative of $f$ at all.</b> It is an
algebraic <em>quadratic</em> constraint $a f^2 + c f + d = 0$, and its two roots are
the two branches of Gauss&ndash;Bonnet gravity (footnote 3 of the paper). The
minus branch is the root with a smooth $\alpha\to0$ limit. It satisfies
$f(r_h)=0$ whenever $b(r_h)=0$, because once $b$ vanishes every remaining term of
the constraint carries a factor of $f$.</li>
<li><b>The rest are linear in $(f',b'',h'',w'')$</b>, as Lovelock's theorem
requires.</li>
</ul>

<p>The $\theta$ check came out more interesting than expected. The $(tt)$, $(rr)$,
$(\theta\theta)$, $(t\varphi)$ and $(\varphi\psi)$ components are literally
identical at $\theta=\pi/6$ and $\theta=\pi/4$ (the last up to an overall factor
of 3). The $(\varphi\varphi)$ component is <em>not</em>, and should not be:
$g_{\varphi\varphi}$ itself depends on $\theta$, so that component is a
$\theta$-dependent combination of the others. It is still a valid equation at the
fixed $\theta$ used, which is how the solver uses it.</p>

<p>Substituting the near-horizon expansion (3.1) shows that the $\varepsilon^0$
and $\varepsilon^1$ coefficients (with $\varepsilon=r-r_h$) vanish
<em>identically</em> for the $(tt)$, $(\theta\theta)$ and $(t\varphi)$ components,
and that the $(rr)$ component starts at order $\varepsilon$. A non-degenerate
horizon with $f=b=0$ is therefore an admissible regular singular point, and the
horizon data are constrained only at order $\varepsilon^2$. <b>That degeneracy is
the central numerical difficulty of this problem</b> &mdash; see &sect;9.</p>

<h2 id="method">4. The numerical method</h2>

<p><b>Variables.</b> The asymptotics (3.2) are subtracted analytically. With
$A=(1-\sqrt{1-2\alpha/\ell^2})/\alpha$,</p>
<pre>f = 1 + A r^2 + P(r)/r^2      P -> f2
b = 1 + A r^2 + Q(r)/r^2      Q -> b2
h =     r^2   + Y(r)/r^2      Y -> l^2 (f2-b2)(1+sqrt(1-2a/l^2))/2
w =           Omega(r)/r^4    Omega -> w4</pre>
<p>so the asymptotic charges are read off directly instead of being extracted as a
cancelling difference of numbers of order $Ar^2\sim10^3$, which at double
precision would destroy them.</p>

<p><b>Grid.</b> Chebyshev&ndash;Gauss&ndash;Lobatto nodes in $x\in[0,1]$ with
$r=r_h/(1-sx)$, $s=1-r_h/R$; the horizon sits exactly on the first node. The
ratio $R/r_h$ sets the dynamic range and it matters: $R=80$, $N=80$ works at
$r_h=0.5$ but not at $r_h=0.3$, nor for the fast-rotating solutions. Figures 2
and 3 use $R=80,N=80$; Figures 1 and 4 use $R=30,N=60$.</p>

<p><b>System.</b> All six derived components are imposed in residual form at every
node except the horizon node, where they vanish identically; seven boundary
conditions are appended:</p>
<pre>f(r_h) = 0     b(r_h) = 0     w(r_h) = w_h
Q'(R) = 0      Omega'(R) = 0   Y'(R) = 0     Y''(R) = 0</pre>
<p>$f(r_h)=0$ is what selects the minus branch of the quadratic constraint.
Without it the Newton solve converges happily to configurations with
$f'(r_h)<0$. The over-determined system is solved in the least-squares sense
with an analytic Jacobian (verified against finite differences to $4\times10^{-12}$).</p>

<p><b>Row scaling.</b> Each equation is a near-perfect cancellation of terms
growing like $r^{12}$, so the size of a raw residual says nothing about how
strongly that equation constrains the solution. Every row is divided by the norm
of its own gradient, frozen during a Newton sweep &mdash; and, crucially, each
residual is first divided by $(r-r_h)^2$ (by $(r-r_h)$ for the $(rr)$ component)
to remove the horizon degeneracy analytically. See &sect;9.</p>

<p><b>Continuation.</b> From the closed forms &mdash; (2.15) when $w_h\neq0$ at
$\alpha=0$, (2.14) when $w_h=0$ &mdash; then continued in $\alpha$, $w_h$ or $r_h$.
For Figure 4, continuation <em>in $r_h$</em> proved fragile, so each $r_h$ is
instead solved independently: seeded from the exact solution at that same $r_h$
and continued in $\alpha$.</p>

<h2 id="figs">5. The figures</h2>
@@figs@@

<h2 id="eps">5a. Point-by-point against the authors' own data</h2>

<div class="box good">
<b>An earlier version of this report said a point-by-point comparison with the
published figures was impossible, because the paper tabulates nothing. That was
wrong.</b> The <code>.eps</code> files distributed with the arXiv source are
gnuplot 3.7 output: every curve is stored as an absolute <code>x y M</code>
followed by relative <code>dx dy V</code> steps, and the axis tick labels are
written as text at known device coordinates. The figures therefore <em>contain
the numbers</em>, and the axes calibrate from the ticks to a residual of
$10^{-16}$. <code>eps_extract.py</code> recovers them; <code>compare_eps.py</code>
compares.
</div>

<p>Each published curve is matched to one of ours by best agreement, then the RMS
difference is taken over the overlapping range and quoted as a fraction of that
curve's vertical span:</p>

<table>
<tr><th>panel</th><th>quantity</th><th>rms diff</th><th>rms / span</th></tr>
<tr><td rowspan="6">Fig 3a</td><td>$f_2$</td><td>2.4e-4</td><td>0.05%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$-b_2$</td><td>3.2e-4</td><td>0.06%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$20\,w_4$</td><td>2.6e-3</td><td>0.21%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$h_h/r_h^2-2$</td><td>2.8e-3</td><td>0.85%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$b_1$</td><td>5.0e-2</td><td><b>1.92%</b></td></tr>
<tr><td>$f_1$</td><td>6.6e-2</td><td><b>2.20%</b></td></tr>
<tr><td rowspan="6">Fig 3b</td><td>$E^{(0)}$</td><td>3.9e-4</td><td>0.06%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$S_{GB}$</td><td>1.3e-3</td><td>0.10%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$-E^{(c)}/10$</td><td>2.2e-4</td><td>0.17%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$10\,J$</td><td>1.8e-3</td><td>0.32%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$S_0$</td><td>1.6e-4</td><td>0.74%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$T_H$</td><td>4.6e-3</td><td><b>2.04%</b></td></tr>
<tr><td rowspan="3">Fig 4a</td><td>$f_2$, $-b_2$, $w_4$</td><td>&lt;3e-4</td><td>&le;0.04%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$h_h/r_h^2-2$</td><td>1.0e-3</td><td>0.85%</td></tr>
<tr><td>$f_1$, $b_1$</td><td>&le;1.0e-2</td><td><b>2.1&ndash;3.5%</b></td></tr>
<tr><td>Fig 4b</td><td>$T_H$, $E^{(0)}$, $J$, $S_0$, $S_{GB}$</td><td>&le;8e-3</td><td>&le;2.5%</td></tr>
</table>

<p>The overlays are in &sect;5 above: the first shows Figures 3 and 4, the
second the profile figures. Figure 2 there is fully like-for-like and the curves
lie on top of each other; in Figure 1 only the static curves are at identical
parameters, and those coincide as well.</p>

<p>So the reproduction is confirmed quantitatively, not just visually &mdash; and
this is also the check that closes the gap identified in &sect;2: the
Gauss&ndash;Bonnet terms <em>with rotation</em>, which no closed form tests, agree
with the authors' results to a fraction of a per cent in every asymptotic and
thermodynamic quantity.</p>

<div class="box warn">
<b>The exception.</b> $f_1=f'(r_h)$ and $b_1=b'(r_h)$ agree only to 2&ndash;3.5%,
and $T_H=\sqrt{f_1b_1}/4\pi$ inherits it. Everything else agrees ten to forty
times better. A reader noticed the symptom before the cause: in an earlier
version those two curves were visibly kinked, i.e. not differentiable in
$\alpha$, which the published ones plainly are.
<br><br>
Part of that was ours. Figures 2 and 3 had been computed at $R=80$, and $f_1,b_1$
are by far the quantities most sensitive to how the grid is distributed.
Recomputing at $R=30$ removed the kinks and cut the error from ~7% to ~2%, while
leaving $f_2$, $b_2$, $w_4$ unchanged in the fifth decimal (third figure in
&sect;5). What remained was a smooth, converged 2&ndash;3% offset.
</div>

<h3>5a-i. Is that offset a mistake in our implementation?</h3>

<p>Asked directly, and the honest answer is: <b>no test we can construct says
so</b>, and two independent tests say the opposite. Neither is conclusive on its
own, but together they locate the difficulty in the quantity rather than in
either calculation.</p>

<p><b>Test 1 &mdash; the paper's own two figures disagree with each other.</b>
Figures 3 and 4 share exactly one solution: $r_h=0.5$, $w_h=0.5$, $\alpha=0.5$,
$\ell^2=20$. Figure 3 reaches it at $\alpha=0.5$, Figure 4 at $r_h=0.5$. Reading
both off the published .eps files:</p>

<table>
<tr><th>quantity</th><th>paper, Fig 3</th><th>paper, Fig 4</th>
    <th>their internal disagreement</th><th>ours</th></tr>
<tr><td>$f_1$</td><td>1.0941</td><td>1.0545</td><td><b>3.63%</b></td><td>1.0643</td></tr>
<tr><td>$b_1$</td><td>1.3532</td><td>1.3146</td><td><b>2.85%</b></td><td>1.3266</td></tr>
<tr><td>$T_H$</td><td>0.0969</td><td>0.0936</td><td><b>3.43%</b></td><td>0.0946</td></tr>
<tr><td>$E^{(0)}$</td><td>0.7607</td><td>0.7681</td><td>0.98%</td><td>0.7607</td></tr>
<tr><td>$f_2$</td><td>&minus;0.5202</td><td>&minus;0.5205</td><td>0.05%</td><td>&minus;0.5203</td></tr>
</table>

<p>The paper disagrees with <em>itself</em> by 3.6% on $f_1$ and 3.4% on $T_H$ at
the one point both figures contain &mdash; the same size as our disagreement with
it &mdash; while agreeing with itself to 0.05% on $f_2$, which is also where we
agree with it to 0.05%. <b>And our value sits between the paper's own two in
every case.</b> The quantities that are hard are hard for both calculations.</p>

<p><b>Test 2 &mdash; the first law.</b> Along Figure 4's family $r_h$ varies at
fixed $\alpha$ and fixed $w_h$, so it is a genuine one-parameter family of
solutions and must satisfy
$dE = T\,dS + 2\Omega\,dJ$ with $\Omega=w_h$; in the paper's plotting units,
$dE = 2\pi T\,dS + 2w_h\,dJ$. This is a real test, because $T$ is built from
$f_1,b_1$ &mdash; the quantities in dispute &mdash; while $E$, $S$ and $J$ are built
from $f_2$, $b_2$, $w_4$ and $h_h$, on which everyone agrees to better than 1%.
Validating the units on the exact $\alpha=0$ family gives a violation of
$1.5\times10^{-5}$, which is the floor set by numerical differentiation. Then:</p>

<table>
<tr><th>$T$ used, with $E,S,J$ from this work</th><th>median violation of the first law</th></tr>
<tr><td>ours</td><td><b>1.2 &times; 10<sup>&minus;5</sup></b></td></tr>
<tr><td>the published curve</td><td>4.1 &times; 10<sup>&minus;3</sup></td></tr>
</table>

<p>a factor of 340. Inverting the relation, the temperature that $E$, $S$ and $J$
<em>demand</em> agrees with ours to a mean ratio of 1.0000 and with the published
curve to 1.0054. Applying the test to the paper's own five curves throughout,
with no input from us, the temperature implied by their $E$, $S$, $J$ exceeds
their plotted $T$ by 3.7%.</p>

<div class="box good">
<b>Conclusion.</b> $f_1$ and $b_1$ are simply the hardest quantities in this
problem &mdash; they are derivatives evaluated at the one point where the field
equations degenerate (&sect;3, &sect;9) &mdash; and they carry a few per cent of
uncertainty in the published calculation as well as in ours. We can find no
error in our implementation, our value lies inside the paper's own spread, and
the first law independently favours our $T_H$. That is as far as the evidence
goes: it is not proof that our number is the right one.
</div>

<h3>5b. The $f/b$ curve of the published Figure 1 is the reciprocal</h3>

<p>A reader noticed that our $f(r)/b(r)$ in Figure 1 <em>rises</em> towards 1
while the published one <em>falls</em> towards 1. It is not a sign error on our
side: the published curve behaves like $b/f$.</p>

<p><b>The argument that relies on nothing but the paper's own figures.</b> When
$w_h=0$ the solution is static, $f\equiv b$, and $f/b=1$ &mdash; the published
Figure 1 shows exactly that for its dashed curve. Switching on rotation, every
other panel of the paper puts $f/b$ <em>below</em> 1:</p>

<table>
<tr><th>published figure</th><th>parameters</th><th>$f/b$ at the horizon</th></tr>
<tr><td>Figure 2</td><td>$\alpha=1$, $w_h=0.5$</td><td>0.6707</td></tr>
<tr><td>Figure 2</td><td>$\alpha=0.1$, $w_h=0.5$</td><td>0.9638</td></tr>
<tr><td>Figure 3a</td><td>$\alpha=0.5$, $w_h=0.5$</td><td>$f_1/b_1=0.8086$</td></tr>
<tr><td><b>Figure 1</b></td><td>$\alpha=0.5$, $w_h=1.8$</td><td><b>1.6904</b></td></tr>
</table>

<p>Our own solutions decrease monotonically in $w_h$ &mdash; $f_1/b_1 = 1$ at
$w_h=0$, 0.66 at $w_h=0.9$, 0.58 at $w_h=1.25$ &mdash; so at $w_h=1.8$ one expects
a number well below 1, not 1.69. Figure 1 is the only panel that goes the other
way.</p>

<p><b>A second, corroborating handle, with a caveat.</b> Eq. (2.15) has
$b=r^2f/h$, so at a horizon where $f$ and $b$ vanish linearly,
$f/b|_{r_h} = h_h/r_h^2$. Figure 1's own $h/r^2+1$ curve reads 1.5913 at the
horizon, i.e. $h_h/r_h^2 = 0.5913$, and $1/0.5913 = 1.6911$ &mdash; the plotted
curve (1.6904) to 0.04%. <em>The caveat</em>: that relation is exact only at
$\alpha=0$. We never impose it (see &sect;5c), and at $\alpha=0.5$ our solutions
violate it by about 4%. So a 0.04% match to its reciprocal is in fact
<em>too</em> good, which suggests the curve may have been generated as $r^2/h$
rather than as an independently computed $b/f$. Either way it is not $f/b$.</p>

<div class="box warn">
We read this as a plotting or labelling slip confined to that one panel: Figures
2 and 3a of the same paper use the convention we do, and the field equations fix
which way up it goes. It is the authors' figure, so we set out the evidence and
leave the conclusion to the reader. Inverting our curve would reproduce the
published shape.
</div>

<h3>5c. Is $b=r^2f/h$ assumed for $\alpha\neq0$?</h3>

<p>No &mdash; it is never used anywhere in the solver. $b$ is an independent
unknown function, discretised on the same grid as $f$, $h$ and $w$ and determined
by its own field equation. The relation is a property of the exact
Myers&ndash;Perry&ndash;AdS$_5$ solution (2.15), which solves the equations only
at $\alpha=0$.</p>

<p>What happens once $\alpha\neq0$ is therefore a <em>result</em>, and it is worth
recording, because it measures how far the Gauss&ndash;Bonnet solutions move away
from the Einstein ones:</p>

<table>
<tr><th>$\alpha$</th><th>$f_1/b_1$</th><th>$h_h/r_h^2$</th><th>violation</th></tr>
<tr><td>0</td><td>1.06579</td><td>1.06579</td><td>$1\times10^{-8}$ (exact)</td></tr>
<tr><td>0.2</td><td>0.90817</td><td>0.93837</td><td>3.2%</td></tr>
<tr><td>0.5</td><td>0.80223</td><td>0.83796</td><td>4.3%</td></tr>
<tr><td>1.0</td><td>0.64915</td><td>0.71328</td><td>9.0%</td></tr>
</table>

<p>Through the bulk rather than at the horizon, $|b-r^2f/h|/|b|$ reaches 5.9% at
$\alpha=1$ and 2.0% at $\alpha=0.1$. That the violation vanishes to $10^{-8}$ at
$\alpha=0$, where it must, is one more check that the solver is doing what it
claims.</p>

<h2 id="wh">6. Why $w_h=1.8$ could not be reached</h2>

<p><b>The short version, without any numerics.</b> Spin a black hole faster while
holding its horizon radius fixed and you drain its surface gravity. In Kerr this
is the familiar bound $a\le M$: past it there is no horizon left, only a naked
singularity. The same thing happens here. The horizon velocity $w_h$ cannot be
raised indefinitely at fixed $r_h$ &mdash; at some $w_h^{\rm ext}$ the temperature
$T_H\propto\sqrt{f'(r_h)b'(r_h)}$ reaches zero, the horizon becomes degenerate,
and beyond that no black hole with that $r_h$ exists for the solver to find.
So the failure to reach $w_h=1.8$ is not a case of the solver giving up on a
hard problem; on our branch there is nothing there to converge to.
<br>
Two things then blur together near the wall, and they are worth separating.
<em>Physically</em>, the family ends. <em>Numerically</em>, our accuracy dies just
<em>before</em> it ends, because $f_1,b_1\to0$ makes the near-horizon rows &mdash;
already the delicate part of this discretisation (&sect;9) &mdash; degenerate
further. So our practical limit sits a little inside the true one: at $\alpha=0$
the true bound is 1.4318 and we stop trusting ourselves around 1.40&ndash;1.43.</p>

<p>At fixed $r_h$ the family of black holes ends at an <b>extremal</b> horizon
velocity, where $f'(r_h),b'(r_h)\to0$ and $T_H\to0$; past it $f'(r_h)<0$ and
$r=r_h$ is no longer an outer horizon.</p>

<p>At $\alpha=0$ this needs no numerics at all, because the family is the exact
solution (2.15). For $r_h=0.5$, $\ell^2=20$ it becomes extremal at
$\hat a = 0.353526$, that is at</p>
<p style="text-align:center;font-size:1.15em">$w_h^{\rm ext} = 1.431782$</p>
<p>so at $\alpha=0$, $w_h=1.8$ is not a black hole. The question is then whether
the solver's failure is its own, and whether $\alpha$ moves the bound.</p>

<p><b>Is the solver at fault?</b> No. Compared against the exact family right up
to the bound:</p>
<pre>alpha = 0, r_h = 0.5, l^2 = 20.  Exact extremal w_h = 1.431782

<p>Eight correct digits up to $w_h=1.2$, and $1.4\times10^{-4}$ at $w_h=1.40$ &mdash;
within 2% of extremality. It only breaks down where $f_1,b_1\to0$, exactly as one
would expect given that the near-horizon rows are the weak link. Independently,
extrapolating $b_1(w_h)$ from the well-converged range $[0.9,1.4]$ returns
1.4318, the exact value to five digits &mdash; which validates the extrapolation
method on a case where the answer is known.</p>

<p><b>Does $\alpha$ move the bound?</b> Barely. At $\alpha=0.5$, the parameters of
Figure 1, $f_1$ and $b_1$ decrease monotonically and both cross zero between
$w_h=1.45$ and $1.50$:</p>

<b>Conclusion.</b> On our branch, $w_h=1.8$ at $r_h=0.5$, $\alpha=0.5$,
$\ell^2=20$ lies beyond extremality. We cannot tell whether the paper normalises
$w$ differently, sits on a different branch, or whether our continuation leaves
the physical branch early. <b>The discrepancy is recorded as unresolved</b>; we do
not assert the paper is wrong on the strength of our own numerics. Figure 1 is
drawn at $w_h=1.25$, the largest value at which every field equation still holds
to $10^{-6}$ relative.
</div>

<p>A caution about method, from the same investigation: the same polynomial
extrapolation that nails the $\alpha=0$ bound to five digits returns <code>nan</code>
at $\alpha=0.5$, and $f_1$/$b_1$ estimates differing by 50% at $\alpha=0.25$.
Those numbers are not quoted anywhere; the $\alpha=0.5$ statement above rests on
direct bracketing, not extrapolation. A method that passes one validation is not
thereby validated everywhere.</p>

<h2 id="acc">7. Accuracy, measured not assumed</h2>

<p>Solving the same configuration ($r_h=0.5$, $w_h=0.5$, $\alpha=0.5$) at two
outer radii:</p>
<pre>--- effect of the outer radius, at r_h = 0.5, alpha = 0.5, w_h = 0.5
    R=  30 N= 60  f1=1.064271 b1=1.326642 hh=0.209491 f2=-0.520314 b2=-0.520330 w4=0.062000
    R=  80 N= 80  f1=1.013254 b1=1.393137 hh=0.209394 f2=-0.520259 b2=-0.520274 w4=0.061981
    f1  relative difference 5.03e-02
    b1  relative difference 4.77e-02
    hh  relative difference 4.62e-04
    f2  relative difference 1.07e-04

<div class="box warn">
$f_2$, $b_2$, $h_h$ and $w_4$ agree to a few parts in $10^4$. But $f_1$ and $b_1$
<em>individually</em> differ by about <b>5%</b> &mdash; while their <em>product</em>,
which is what $T_H$ depends on, agrees to $2\times10^{-4}$. So the $f_1$ and $b_1$
curves in Figures 3a and 4a carry a few per cent of numerical uncertainty and
every other plotted quantity is good to $\sim10^{-4}$. The paper reports
$10^{-8}$ relative accuracy for its own collocation solutions; we are not there.
</div>

<h2 id="notdone">8. What was not reproduced, and not checked</h2>

<p><b>Not reproduced.</b></p>
<ul>
<li>Figure 1 at $w_h=1.8$ &mdash; &sect;6. Drawn at $w_h=1.25$.</li>
<li>Figure 4 below $r_h\approx0.3$. The published figure starts near $r_h=0.15$;
our solves below 0.30 fail the linearity test at the horizon. The paper itself
notes that &ldquo;for small values of $r_h$ the numerical analysis is quite
tedious&rdquo;.</li>
<li>The two-branch structure in $w_h$ described at the end of Section 4.</li>
</ul>

<p><b>Not checked.</b></p>
<ul>
<li>No point-by-point comparison with the published curves is possible: the paper
tabulates nothing.</li>
<li>Figures 3 and 4 are drawn with the published axis limits, so a curve that
leaves the frame does so here and not necessarily in the original.</li>
<li>The counterterm coefficients $c_1,c_2$ of Eq. (2.9) and the boundary stress
tensor (2.10)&ndash;(2.11) were <em>not</em> re-derived; deriving them needs the
boundary variational calculus, not the bulk equations. The charge formulas
(3.6)&ndash;(3.7) are used as the paper gives them. What is checked is that they
return the exact Casimir energy $3\ell^2/8$ at $\alpha=0$ and the closed-form
static entropy $S=r_h^3+3\alpha r_h$.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="bugs">9. Five bugs, and the one that bit three times</h2>

<p>Recorded because each one produced <em>plausible-looking</em> output, and
because the last is a trap anyone solving this system will fall into.</p>

<ol>
<li><b>Wrong index placement in $H_{\mu\nu}$ &mdash; a bug in our sympy code.</b>
To be explicit, since this is about our program and not about the paper:
Eq. (2.4) contains the term $R_{\mu\sigma\kappa\tau}R_\nu{}^{\sigma\kappa\tau}$,
in which the second factor has its <em>first</em> index down and the last three
up. In <code>derive_eqs.py</code> we first built that factor from an array
holding $R^{\nu p}{}_{qu}$ &mdash; i.e. with the first <em>two</em> indices raised
&mdash; instead of taking $R_{\nu p q u}$ and raising only the last three. The
correction is the single line now reading
<code>B = sum(Ginv[s_,p]*Rdn[nu,p,q,u]*Ginv[k,q]*Ginv[tt,u] ...)</code>, where
<code>Rdn</code> is the fully lowered Riemann tensor.
<br>
Symptom: the derived equations came out <em>quadratic</em> in the second
derivatives, which violates the quasi-linearity Lovelock's theorem guarantees.
Caught by a numerical linearity test (second differences in $b''$, $h''$, $w''$
should vanish), not by reading the code. After the fix the equations shrank from
~2800 to ~170 operations for the $(rr)$ component, and the closed-form solutions
satisfied them identically.</li>
<li><b>Wrong horizon mass for the static solution &mdash; again our code, since
corrected.</b> This entry describes a bug we made and then fixed; the wrong
expression below is <em>not</em> what the code does now, which has caused
confusion, so both are spelled out.
<br><br>
Eq. (2.14) is
$f = 1 + \frac{r^2}{\alpha}\left(1-\sqrt{1+2\alpha\left(\frac{m}{r^4}-\frac{1}{\ell^2}\right)}\right)$,
and to build the static starting configuration we need the $m$ that puts the
horizon at $r_h$, i.e. that solves $f(r_h)=0$. Rearranging,
$\frac{r_h^2}{\alpha}\left(\sqrt{\cdot}-1\right)=1$, so
<div style="margin:.5rem 0 .5rem 1.2rem">
<span style="color:#c33">what we first coded (wrong):</span>
&nbsp; $\sqrt{\;\cdot\;} = 1 + \dfrac{r_h^{2}}{\alpha}$ <br>
<span style="color:#2a2">what it should be, and what the code does now:</span>
&nbsp; $\sqrt{\;\cdot\;} = 1 + \dfrac{\alpha}{r_h^{2}}$
</div>
The corrected version is the one obtained by hand by a reader of this report, and
sympy confirms it: solving $f(r_h)=0$ symbolically gives the closed form
<div style="text-align:center">$m = \dfrac{\alpha}{2} + r_h^{2} + \dfrac{r_h^{4}}{\ell^{2}}$</div>
which is exactly what <code>egb_exact.static_gb_horizon_mass</code> computes, and
$f(r_h)$ evaluates to $0$ to $10^{-16}$ at every parameter set tested
(<code>scratch/audit_inversions.py</code>). The analogous inversion for MPAdS$_5$
was audited the same way and is correct.
<br>
Symptom of the original bug: the static seed was not a solution at all, so every
$w_h$ continuation started from the wrong configuration. It was caught by
comparing the "static" solve against the closed form.</li>
<li><b>The branch condition was missing.</b> $b(r_h)=0$ alone leaves both roots of
the quadratic constraint available; the solver returned $f'(r_h)<0$ with a tiny
residual. Fixed by imposing $f(r_h)=0$ explicitly &mdash; in the $(rr)$ row at the
horizon node, which is vacuous there anyway.</li>
<li><b>Grid transfer during $r_h$ continuation.</b> Interpolating the previous
solution in $r$ smears the horizon region and throws Newton onto an unphysical
branch. Since consecutive grids share the same computational nodes $x$, the
correct transfer is the identity in $x$.</li>
<li><b>The outer radius.</b> $R/r_h$ is the grid's dynamic range; $R=80$ silently
degrades at $r_h=0.3$.</li>
</ol>

<div class="box bad">
<b>The one that bit three times.</b> Three separate times the solver reported
residuals of $10^{-20}$ &ndash; $10^{-25}$ together with horizon data that were
pure noise ($f_1=-16$, $b_1=47$, $h_h<0$), or with $f$ and $b$ sitting at
$10^{-12}$ over the first several nodes instead of vanishing linearly.
<br><br>
Every time the cause was the same shape of error: <b>the rows near the horizon
carry no weight</b>, because every field equation vanishes like $(r-r_h)^2$ there.
Normalising residuals by their own magnitude, or putting a floor under that
scale, silently deletes exactly the equations that pin the horizon. Remove the
floor and the solver instead fits amplified round-off.
<br><br>
The cure is to divide the zero out <em>analytically</em> &mdash; each residual by
$(r-r_h)^2$, the $(rr)$ one by $(r-r_h)$ &mdash; and only then equilibrate rows by
the norm of their own gradient.
<br><br>
<b>The lesson worth keeping: a tiny residual is not evidence of a solution when
the residual has been normalised by something that itself vanishes.</b> The
diagnostic that actually caught it was not the residual at all, but checking that
$f(r)/(r-r_h) \to f'(r_h)$ near the horizon.
</div>

<p>A related trap, found later: that same linearity diagnostic <em>fails
legitimately</em> near extremality, because $f_1\to0$ makes higher-order terms
dominate at any fixed node. Used as a rejection test it was over-conservative and
threw away good solutions. Tests have domains of validity too.</p>

<h2 id="appendix">Appendix. The numerical method, in plain terms</h2>

<h3>A.1 What has to be solved</h3>
<p>After the reduction, the unknowns are four functions of one variable,
$f,b,h,w$ on $r\in[r_h,\infty)$. Three of the equations are second order in
$b,h,w$; $f$ is fixed pointwise by the algebraic $(rr)$ constraint. This is a
<em>boundary-value</em> problem, not an initial-value one: conditions are imposed
at both ends (regularity and $w=w_h$ at the horizon, prescribed asymptotics at
infinity), so one cannot simply integrate outward from $r_h$.</p>

<h3>A.2 Why not just shoot?</h3>
<p>The obvious method is shooting: guess the missing horizon data, integrate
outward with a Runge&ndash;Kutta solver, see how badly you miss the conditions at
infinity, adjust, repeat. Two things spoil it here. First, $r=r_h$ is a
<em>singular</em> point of the system: $f$ and $b$ both vanish there, and writing
the equations in the explicit form $y'=g(y)$ requires inverting a matrix that
becomes singular exactly at the horizon (we measured its condition number
blowing up like $1/\varepsilon^2$). Second, the unwanted asymptotic modes grow
with $r$, so small errors at the horizon are amplified on the way out.</p>

<h3>A.3 Collocation: turn the ODEs into algebra</h3>
<p>Collocation avoids both. Instead of marching, you represent each unknown
function by its <em>values at a fixed set of points</em> &mdash; here $N+1$
Chebyshev&ndash;Gauss&ndash;Lobatto nodes, which cluster towards the ends of the
interval. Derivatives at those nodes are then linear combinations of the values:
a single dense matrix $D$ with $u'\approx Du$, exact for polynomials up to degree
$N$ and spectrally accurate for smooth functions. Substituting into the field
equations turns each differential equation, at each node, into one algebraic
equation. The whole boundary-value problem becomes one large system of nonlinear
algebraic equations in the $4(N+1)$ unknown nodal values &mdash; and because the
horizon is just another node where the (polynomial) equations are perfectly
finite, the singularity is no longer an obstacle.</p>

<h3>A.3a What exactly are $P$, $Q$, $Y$, $\Omega$? (they are not constants)</h3>

<p>A natural misreading, worth heading off. Eq. (3.2) says
$f = 1 + Ar^2 + f_2/r^2 + O(1/r^4)$, and we define $P$ by
$f = 1 + Ar^2 + P(r)/r^2$. It can look as though $P$ has been <em>defined</em> to
be the constant $f_2$. It has not.</p>

<p>$P$, $Q$, $Y$ and $\Omega$ are unknown <b>functions of $r$</b>, carried as
$N+1$ nodal values each, exactly like $f,b,h,w$ themselves. Eq. (3.2) is only the
leading asymptotic behaviour, so what is true is
$$P(r) = f_2 + \frac{f_4}{r^2} + \dots \xrightarrow[r\to\infty]{} f_2 ,$$
a limit, not an identity. At finite $r$, and especially near the horizon, $P$
varies a great deal: $f(r_h)=0$ forces $P(r_h) = -r_h^2(1+Ar_h^2)$, which is a
definite non-zero number fixed by the horizon condition. For the $\alpha=1$
solution of Figure 2, for instance,</p>

<table>
<tr><th>$r$</th><td>0.500</td><td>0.535</td><td>0.663</td><td>0.984</td><td>1.905</td><td>30.0</td></tr>
<tr><th>$P(r)$</th><td>&minus;0.2532</td><td>&minus;0.2846</td><td>&minus;0.3941</td>
    <td>&minus;0.5997</td><td>&minus;0.7674</td><td>&minus;0.7900</td></tr>
</table>

<p>&mdash; a factor of three between the horizon and the outer boundary, flattening
onto $f_2=-0.7897$ only at the far end. The substitution is a change of
variables, not an ansatz: it buys two things and assumes nothing. It makes the
unknowns $O(1)$ instead of $O(r^2)$, and it puts the quantity we actually want,
$f_2$, at a single node ($P$ at $r=R$) instead of requiring us to extract it from
the difference of two large nearly-cancelling numbers. The boundary conditions
$Q'(R)=\Omega'(R)=Y'(R)=0$ are precisely the statement "these functions have
gone flat by the outer boundary", i.e. that the asymptotic regime has been
reached &mdash; and they would be vacuous if the functions were constants by
construction.</p>

<h3>A.4 Newton, and what a "Newton sweep" means here</h3>

<p><b>First, what a "row" is.</b> After collocation the whole problem is one
vector equation $F(u)=0$. The unknown vector is
$$u = \big(P_0,\dots,P_N,\;Q_0,\dots,Q_N,\;Y_0,\dots,Y_N,\;\Omega_0,\dots,\Omega_N\big)
\in\mathbb{R}^{4(N+1)},$$
the nodal values. The <b>residual</b> $F(u)$ is built like this: from $u$ we
reconstruct $f,b,h,w$ and their derivatives at every node, using the definitions
<a href="#eqS">(S)</a> for the values and the differentiation matrix $D$ for the
derivatives; we substitute those into the left-hand side of each of the six
derived field equations; and we collect the results. So</p>
<div style="text-align:center">$F_i(u) \;=\;$ (equation $k$, evaluated at node
$j$), &nbsp; divided by $(r_j-r_h)^2$ and by its row weight,</div>
<p>with one such entry for every pair $(k,j)$, plus seven further entries holding
the boundary conditions <a href="#eqBC">(BC)</a>. A <b>row</b> is one of these scalar entries
&mdash; one equation at one point &mdash; and correspondingly one row of the Jacobian
$J_{i m}=\partial F_i/\partial u_m$. Solving the discretised problem means
finding $u$ with $F(u)=0$, and since there are more rows than unknowns (six
equations per node, four unknowns per node) we minimise $\|F(u)\|^2$ instead.</p>

<p><b>Why "the rows near the horizon carry no weight".</b> Least squares
minimises $\sum_i \big(F_i/w_i\big)^2$, so a row divided by a large weight $w_i$
contributes almost nothing to the sum: the solver is then free to violate that
equation at no cost. Now, every field equation vanishes like $(r-r_h)^2$ at the
horizon, so at the nodes nearest $r_h$ the raw residuals are tiny <em>whatever
the solution looks like there</em>. Scale each row by its own magnitude and put a
floor under the scale &mdash; which is what we did, twice &mdash; and those rows get
divided by something far larger than themselves; they drop out of the sum, and
the near-horizon part of the solution becomes unconstrained. That is exactly the
failure in &sect;9: residuals of $10^{-25}$ next to horizon data that were noise.
Remove the floor instead and the same rows are divided by something vanishing,
which amplifies round-off to $O(1)$ and the solver fits the noise. Neither
extreme works; the cure is to cancel the $(r-r_h)^2$ analytically first, and only
then scale each row by the norm of its own gradient, which measures how strongly
that equation constrains $u$ rather than how big it happens to be.</p>

<p><b>Newton.</b> With $F$ defined, Newton's method linearises about the current
guess, $F(u+\delta)\approx F(u)+J\delta$, solves $J\delta=-F(u)$ in the
least-squares sense, steps to $u+\delta$, and repeats until $F$ is at round-off.
We supply $J$ analytically &mdash; the chain rule through <a href="#eqS">(S)</a> and
through $D$ &mdash; which is both faster and more accurate than finite-differencing
some 250 columns; it agrees with a central-difference Jacobian to
$4\times10^{-12}$.</p>
<p><b>Now the phrase itself.</b> The row scaling just described depends on the
solution, and letting it change during the iteration would destroy Newton's
quadratic convergence &mdash; the residual would no longer be a fixed function
being driven to zero. So the weights are computed once, held <b>frozen</b> while
Newton iterates to convergence, then recomputed from the new solution, and Newton
run again. <b>One such cycle &mdash; freeze the weights, iterate Newton to
convergence, recompute the weights &mdash; is what is meant here by a "Newton
sweep".</b> Three sweeps are used; in practice the solution stops moving after
the second.</p>

<h3>A.5 Continuation</h3>
<p>Newton only converges from a good enough starting guess, and for these
equations there is no good guess at, say, $\alpha=1$. So we start where an exact
solution is known &mdash; Eq. (2.15) at $\alpha=0$, or Eq. (2.14) at $w_h=0$ &mdash;
and walk the parameter in small steps, each solve seeded with the previous
answer. This is the standard trick, and it is what the paper describes doing in
its Section 4. It also explains a failure mode we hit: if a step is too large, or
if the transfer between grids is sloppy, Newton converges to a
<em>different</em> solution of the same equations &mdash; one that is mathematically
valid but not a black hole (see the $f'(r_h)<0$ branch in &sect;9).</p>

<h3>A.6 What this method does <em>not</em> give you</h3>
<p>It gives no error estimate. A converged Newton solve says the residual is at
round-off <em>for the discretisation you chose</em>; it says nothing about whether
that discretisation resolves the problem. All the accuracy statements in this
report therefore come from outside the solver: comparison with closed-form
solutions, variation of $N$ and $R$, and comparison with the authors' published
data.</p>

<h2 id="code">11. The source files</h2>
<p>All files are also in <code>code/</code> next to this page. Click to expand.</p>
@@code@@

</html>
"""

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

The four published figures are drawn from `figdata.npz` (produced by
`make_figures.py`).  Every figure also has a live version whose parameters
(r_h, w_h, alpha, l^2, grid size) can be varied with the sliders: those panels
re-solve the field equations on the spot, so the figures are not hard-wired to

@app.cell
def _(N_s, Z, al_s, go, l2_s, mo, np, plt, rh_s, wh_s):
    def _live():
        if not go.value:
            return mo.md('*press **solve***')
        rh, wh = rh_s.value, wh_s.value
        al, l2, N = al_s.value, l2_s.value, N_s.value
        if al > l2/2:
            return mo.md(r'$\alpha>\ell^2/2$: the theory is undefined here (Sec. 3).')
        steps = max(2, int(round(al/0.05)) + 1)
        res = Z.continue_in('alpha', np.linspace(0.0, al, steps),
                            rh=rh, wh=wh, alpha=0.0, ell2=l2, N=N, R=80.0)
        s, info = res[-1][1], res[-1][2]
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.5))
        x = np.log10(s.r); r = s.r
        ax.plot(x, s.F['h']/r**2 + 1, label=r'$h/r^2+1$')
        ax.plot(x, s.F['f']/s.F['b'], label=r'$f/b$')
        ax.plot(x, s.F['b'], label=r'$b$')
        ax.plot(x, s.F['w'], label=r'$w$')
        ax.plot(x, s.F['bp'] - 2, label=r"$b'-2$")
        ax.set_xlim(np.log10(rh) - 0.02, 1.0); ax.set_ylim(-2.5, 2.5)
        ax.set_xlabel(r'$\log_{10}(r)$'); ax.legend(ncol=5, fontsize=8)
        ax.grid(alpha=.25)
        txt = (f'residual cost {info.cost:.2e}\n\n'
               f'| quantity | value |\n|---|---|\n'
               f'| $f_1$ | {s.f1:.6f} |\n| $b_1$ | {s.b1:.6f} |\n'
               f'| $h_h$ | {s.hh:.6f} |\n| $f_2$ | {s.f2:.6f} |\n'
               f'| $b_2$ | {s.b2:.6f} |\n| $w_4$ | {s.w4:.6f} |\n'
               f'| $T_H$ | {s.T:.6f} |\n| $E^{{(0)}}$ | {s.E0:.6f} |\n'
               f'| $E^{{(c)}}$ | {s.Ec:.6f} |\n| $J$ | {s.J:.6f} |\n'
               f'| $S_0$ | {s.S0:.6f} |\n| $S_{{GB}}$ | {s.SGB:.6f} |\n')
        return mo.hstack([mo.as_html(ax), mo.md(txt)])
    _live()
    return

    app.run()
rank_test.py — Which components of Eq. (2.3) form an independent set. (44 lines)
"""Which components of Eq. (2.3) form an independent set for this ansatz?

The collocation Jacobian is built from every 4-element subset of the six derived
components and its numerical rank is measured at the exact alpha = 0 solution.
A subset whose Jacobian is full rank is a usable system; a rank-deficient one
means the components chosen are not independent (or do not constrain the
unknowns), which is exactly the failure that produced garbage horizon data in a
first attempt.
"""
import itertools
import numpy as np
import egb_solve as Z
import egb_system as S

rh, wh, l2 = 0.5, 0.5, 20.0


def rank_of(order, N=30):
    Z._FUNC_CACHE.clear()
    S.EQNAMES[:] = list(order)
    g = Z.Grid(rh, 80.0, N)
    eg = Z.EGB(0.0, l2)
    u = Z.guess_mpads(g, rh, wh, l2)
    eg.set_weights(g, u, wh)
    J = eg.jacobian(g, u, wh)
    cs = np.linalg.norm(J, axis=0); cs[cs == 0] = 1
    s = np.linalg.svd(J/cs, compute_uv=False)
    return (s > 1e-9*s[0]).sum(), len(s), s[0]/s[-1]


if __name__ == '__main__':
    ALL = ['tt', 'rr', 'thth', 'tph', 'phph', 'phps']
    print('%-32s %s' % ('components (order: tt-slot, rr-slot, thth-slot, tph-slot)',
                        'rank / size   cond'))
    for combo in itertools.permutations(ALL, 4):
        if combo[1] != 'rr':
            continue          # the (rr) slot must hold the algebraic constraint
        try:
            rk, n, c = rank_of(combo)
        except Exception as exc:
            print('%-32s FAILED %s' % (','.join(combo), exc)); continue
        flag = 'FULL RANK' if rk == n else ''
        print('%-32s %4d / %4d  %.1e  %s' % (','.join(combo), rk, n, c, flag))
eps_extract.py — Recovers the plotted coordinates from the authors' gnuplot .eps figures. (150 lines)
"""Extract the published curves from the authors' gnuplot EPS figures.

The .eps files shipped with arXiv:0801.1021 are gnuplot 3.7 output, which draws
every curve as an absolute `x y M` (moveto) followed by relative `dx dy V`
(rlineto) steps, and writes the axis tick labels as text at known device
coordinates.  So the figures are not just pictures: the plotted numbers are in
them, and the axes can be calibrated from the ticks.

This turns the comparison with the paper from "the curves look alike" into an
actual point-by-point comparison.

Usage:
    from eps_extract import load_figure
    fig = load_figure('.../0801.1021 var-alfa1.eps')
    fig['curves']  -> list of dicts with 'x', 'y' arrays in data coordinates
"""
import os
import re

import numpy as np

NUM = r'-?\d+\.?\d*'


def _tokenize(path):
    with open(path, 'r', errors='replace') as fh:
        return fh.read()


def parse_paths(text):
    """Return the polylines, in device coordinates, with their gnuplot line type."""
    paths, cur, lt = [], [], None
    x = y = 0.0
    for raw in text.splitlines():
        line = raw.strip()
        m = re.match(r'^(LT[ab0-9])\b', line)
        if m:
            if len(cur) > 1:
                paths.append((lt, np.array(cur)))
            cur, lt = [], m.group(1)
            continue
        if line.startswith('stroke') or line.startswith('newpath'):
            if len(cur) > 1:
                paths.append((lt, np.array(cur)))
            cur = []
            continue
        m = re.match(r'^(%s)\s+(%s)\s+M$' % (NUM, NUM), line)
        if m:
            if len(cur) > 1:
                paths.append((lt, np.array(cur)))
            x, y = float(m.group(1)), float(m.group(2))
            cur = [(x, y)]
            continue
        m = re.match(r'^(%s)\s+(%s)\s+V$' % (NUM, NUM), line)
        if m:
            x += float(m.group(1)); y += float(m.group(2))
            cur.append((x, y))
            continue
        m = re.match(r'^(%s)\s+(%s)\s+L$' % (NUM, NUM), line)
        if m:
            x, y = float(m.group(1)), float(m.group(2))
            cur.append((x, y))
            continue
        m = re.match(r'^(%s)\s+(%s)\s+R$' % (NUM, NUM), line)
        if m:                                  # rmoveto: breaks the polyline
            if len(cur) > 1:
                paths.append((lt, np.array(cur)))
            x += float(m.group(1)); y += float(m.group(2))
            cur = [(x, y)]
            continue
    if len(cur) > 1:
        paths.append((lt, np.array(cur)))
    return paths


def parse_ticks(text):
    """Axis calibration from the tick labels.

    gnuplot writes  `X Y M`  then a bracketed text block ending in MRshow (right
    aligned -> y axis) or MCshow (centred -> x axis).
    """
    lines = text.splitlines()
    yt, xt = [], []
    for i, raw in enumerate(lines):
        m = re.match(r'^(%s)\s+(%s)\s+M$' % (NUM, NUM), raw.strip())
        if not m:
            continue
        blob = '\n'.join(lines[i + 1:i + 4])
        lab = re.search(r'\(\s*(-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*\)\]', blob)
        if not lab:
            continue
        val = float(lab.group(1))
        if 'MRshow' in blob:
            yt.append((float(m.group(2)), val))
        elif 'MCshow' in blob:
            xt.append((float(m.group(1)), val))
    return xt, yt


def _fit(ticks):
    """Least squares device -> data (they are exactly linear)."""
    d = np.array([t[0] for t in ticks], float)
    v = np.array([t[1] for t in ticks], float)
    A = np.vstack([d, np.ones_like(d)]).T
    coef, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(A, v, rcond=None)
    resid = np.abs(A @ coef - v).max()
    return coef, resid


def load_figure(path, min_points=8):
    text = _tokenize(path)
    xt, yt = parse_ticks(text)
    if len(xt) < 2 or len(yt) < 2:
        raise RuntimeError('could not calibrate axes of %s '
                           '(%d x-ticks, %d y-ticks)' % (path, len(xt), len(yt)))
    (ax, bx), rx = _fit(xt)
    (ay, by), ry = _fit(yt)
    curves = []
    for lt, pts in parse_paths(text):
        if len(pts) < min_points:
            continue                    # ticks, frame, legend keys
        X = ax*pts[:, 0] + bx
        Y = ay*pts[:, 1] + by
        curves.append(dict(lt=lt, x=X, y=Y, n=len(X)))
    return dict(file=os.path.basename(path), curves=curves,
                xticks=sorted(v for _, v in xt), yticks=sorted(v for _, v in yt),
                calib_resid=(rx, ry))


if __name__ == '__main__':
    import sys
    base = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else \
        os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(
            os.path.abspath(__file__)))), 'papers')
    for fn in sorted(os.listdir(base)):
        if not fn.endswith('.eps'):
            continue
        try:
            f = load_figure(os.path.join(base, fn))
        except RuntimeError as exc:
            print('%-42s FAILED %s' % (fn, exc)); continue
        print('%-42s x-ticks %s' % (fn, f['xticks']))
        print('%-42s y-ticks %s  calib residual %.2e/%.2e'
              % ('', f['yticks'], *f['calib_resid']))
        for c in f['curves']:
            print('    %-4s n=%4d  x:[%8.4f,%8.4f]  y:[%8.4f,%8.4f]'
                  % (c['lt'], c['n'], c['x'].min(), c['x'].max(),
                     c['y'].min(), c['y'].max()))
        print()
compare_eps.py — Point-by-point comparison against those coordinates. (153 lines)
"""Point-by-point comparison against the authors' own figure files.

The .eps files distributed with arXiv:0801.1021 are gnuplot output and therefore
contain the plotted coordinates, not just a picture of them (see
`eps_extract.py`).  So the claim "the paper tabulates nothing, therefore only a
visual comparison is possible" was wrong: the published curves can be recovered
as numbers and compared with ours directly.

For each published curve we find the quantity it corresponds to by matching it
against our computed curves, then report the RMS and maximum difference over the
overlapping range.

Run:  python compare_eps.py
"""
import os

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment

from eps_extract import load_figure

PAPERS = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(
    os.path.abspath(__file__)))), 'papers')

# what each published panel plots, and how to build the same thing from our data
PANELS = {
    'var-alfa1': dict(
        eps='0801.1021 var-alfa1.eps', xkey='f3_alpha', title='Figure 3a',
        series=[('f1',        lambda d: d['f3_f1']),
                ('b1',        lambda d: d['f3_b1']),
                ('hh/rh^2-2', lambda d: d['f3_hh']/0.25 - 2),
                ('f2',        lambda d: d['f3_f2']),
                ('-b2',       lambda d: -d['f3_b2']),
                ('20*w4',     lambda d: 20*d['f3_w4'])]),
    'var-alfa2': dict(
        eps='0801.1021 var-alfa2.eps', xkey='f3_alpha', title='Figure 3b',
        series=[('T_H',       lambda d: d['f3_T']),
                ('E0',        lambda d: d['f3_E0']),
                ('-Ec/10',    lambda d: -d['f3_Ec']/10),
                ('10*J',      lambda d: 10*d['f3_J']),
                ('S0',        lambda d: d['f3_S0']),
                ('S_GB',      lambda d: d['f3_SGB'])]),
    'var-rh1': dict(
        eps='0801.1021 var-rh1.eps', xkey='f4_rh', title='Figure 4a',
        series=[('f1',        lambda d: d['f4_f1']),
                ('b1',        lambda d: d['f4_b1']),
                ('hh/rh^2-2', lambda d: d['f4_hh']/d['f4_rh']**2 - 2),
                ('f2',        lambda d: d['f4_f2']),
                ('-b2',       lambda d: -d['f4_b2']),
                ('w4',        lambda d: d['f4_w4'])]),
    'var-rh2': dict(
        eps='0801.1021 var-rh2.eps', xkey='f4_rh', title='Figure 4b',
        series=[('T_H',       lambda d: d['f4_T']),
                ('E0',        lambda d: d['f4_E0']),
                ('-J',        lambda d: -d['f4_J']),
                ('S0',        lambda d: d['f4_S0']),
                ('S_GB',      lambda d: d['f4_SGB'])]),
}


def resample(c, xq):
    """The published curve, interpolated onto our abscissae (inside its range)."""
    o = np.argsort(c['x'])
    x, y = c['x'][o], c['y'][o]
    keep = (xq >= x.min() - 1e-9) & (xq <= x.max() + 1e-9)
    return keep, np.interp(xq[keep], x, y)


def compare(panel, d, verbose=True):
    P = PANELS[panel]
    fig = load_figure(os.path.join(PAPERS, P['eps']))
    xq = d[P['xkey']]
    ours = [(nm, fn(d)) for nm, fn in P['series']]
    pub = [c for c in fig['curves'] if c['n'] >= 15]

    # assign published curves to our series by best RMS agreement
    cost = np.full((len(pub), len(ours)), 1e6)
    inter = {}
    for i, c in enumerate(pub):
        for j, (nm, y) in enumerate(ours):
            keep, yp = resample(c, xq)
            if keep.sum() < 5:
                continue
            dif = yp - y[keep]
            # scale by the spread of the published curve, so big and small
            # quantities are matched on equal footing
            s = max(np.ptp(c['y']), 1e-3)
            cost[i, j] = np.sqrt(np.mean(dif**2))/s
            inter[(i, j)] = (keep, yp)
    ri, cj = linear_sum_assignment(cost)

    rows = []
    for i, j in zip(ri, cj):
        if (i, j) not in inter:
            continue
        nm, y = ours[j]
        keep, yp = inter[(i, j)]
        dif = yp - y[keep]
        rows.append(dict(name=nm, n=int(keep.sum()),
                         rms=float(np.sqrt(np.mean(dif**2))),
                         mx=float(np.abs(dif).max()),
                         span=float(np.ptp(yp)),
                         rel=float(np.sqrt(np.mean(dif**2))/max(np.ptp(yp), 1e-9)),
                         ours_end=(float(y[keep][0]), float(y[keep][-1])),
                         pub_end=(float(yp[0]), float(yp[-1]))))
    if verbose:
        print('%s  (%s)' % (P['title'], P['eps']))
        print('  %-10s %4s %10s %10s %9s   %-22s %-22s'
              % ('quantity', 'n', 'rms diff', 'max diff', 'rms/span',
                 'ours (first,last)', 'paper (first,last)'))
        for r in sorted(rows, key=lambda r: -r['rel']):
            print('  %-10s %4d %10.2e %10.2e %8.2f%%   %-22s %-22s'
                  % (r['name'], r['n'], r['rms'], r['mx'], 100*r['rel'],
                     '%.4f, %.4f' % r['ours_end'], '%.4f, %.4f' % r['pub_end']))
        print()
    return rows


def published_at(panel, x0, d=None):
    """The published value of every curve in a panel at one abscissa, keyed by
    the name of the quantity.  Uses the same assignment as compare()."""
    d = d if d is not None else dict(np.load('figdata.npz'))
    P = PANELS[panel]
    fig = load_figure(os.path.join(PAPERS, P['eps']))
    xq = d[P['xkey']]
    ours = [(nm, fn(d)) for nm, fn in P['series']]
    pub = [c for c in fig['curves'] if c['n'] >= 15]
    cost = np.full((len(pub), len(ours)), 1e6)
    for i, c in enumerate(pub):
        for j, (nm, y) in enumerate(ours):
            keep, yp = resample(c, xq)
            if keep.sum() >= 5:
                cost[i, j] = np.sqrt(np.mean((yp - y[keep])**2))/max(np.ptp(c['y']), 1e-3)
    ri, cj = linear_sum_assignment(cost)
    out = {}
    for i, j in zip(ri, cj):
        c = pub[i]
        o = np.argsort(c['x'])
        out[ours[j][0]] = float(np.interp(x0, c['x'][o], c['y'][o]))
    return out


def main():
    d = dict(np.load('figdata.npz'))
    out = {}
    for panel in ('var-alfa1', 'var-alfa2', 'var-rh1', 'var-rh2'):
        out[panel] = compare(panel, d)
    return out


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
overlay.py — Draws our curves on top of the published ones. (55 lines)
"""Overlay our computed curves on the authors' own published curves, extracted
from the .eps files.  This is the actual reproduction test."""
import os
import numpy as np
import matplotlib
matplotlib.use('Agg')
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from eps_extract import load_figure
from compare_eps import PANELS, PAPERS, resample
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment


def overlay(panel, d, ax):
    P = PANELS[panel]
    fig = load_figure(os.path.join(PAPERS, P['eps']))
    xq = d[P['xkey']]
    ours = [(nm, fn(d)) for nm, fn in P['series']]
    pub = [c for c in fig['curves'] if c['n'] >= 15]
    cost = np.full((len(pub), len(ours)), 1e6)
    for i, c in enumerate(pub):
        for j, (nm, y) in enumerate(ours):
            keep, yp = resample(c, xq)
            if keep.sum() < 5:
                continue
            cost[i, j] = np.sqrt(np.mean((yp - y[keep])**2))/max(np.ptp(c['y']), 1e-3)
    ri, cj = linear_sum_assignment(cost)
    for k, (i, j) in enumerate(zip(ri, cj)):
        nm, y = ours[j]
        c = pub[i]
        o = np.argsort(c['x'])
        ax.plot(c['x'][o], c['y'][o], '-', color='0.55', lw=3.2,
                zorder=1, label='published' if k == 0 else None)
        ax.plot(xq, y, '--', color='C%d' % (j % 10), lw=1.4, zorder=2,
                label='this work' if k == 0 else None)
        m = int(0.62*len(xq))
        ax.annotate(nm, (xq[m], y[m]), fontsize=8, color='C%d' % (j % 10))
    ax.set_xlabel(P['xkey'].split('_')[1]); ax.grid(alpha=.25)
    ax.set_title(P['title'] + '  (grey = paper, dashed = this work)', fontsize=10)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='best')


def main():
    d = dict(np.load('figdata.npz'))
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 9))
    for ax, panel in zip(axs.ravel(), ('var-alfa1', 'var-alfa2', 'var-rh1', 'var-rh2')):
        overlay(panel, d, ax)
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig('fig_overlay.png', dpi=140)
    print('wrote fig_overlay.png')


if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()
